    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Under the protection of Magadharāja, Jarāsandha, the powerful Kaṁsa began persecuting the kings of the Yadu dynasty. In this he had the cooperation of demons like Pralamba, Baka, Cāṇūra, Tṛṇāvarta, Aghāsura, Muṣṭika, Ariṣṭa, Dvivida, Pūtanā, Keśī, Dhenuka, Bāṇāsura, Narakāsura and many other demoniac kings on the surface of the earth.
    Purport

    This verse supports the following statement given by the Lord in Bhagavad-gītā (4.7-8): yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge “Whenever and wherever there is a decline in religious practice, O descendant of Bharata, and a predominant rise of irreligion — at that time I descend Myself. To deliver the pious and to annihilate the miscreants, as well as to reestablish the principles of religion, I Myself appear millennium after millennium.” The Lord’s purpose in maintaining this material world is to give everyone a chance to go back home, back to Godhead, but kings and political leaders unfortunately try to hinder the purpose of the Lord, and therefore the Lord appears, either personally or with His plenary portions, to set things right. It is therefore said: garbhaṁ sañcārya rohiṇyāṁ devakyā yogamāyayā tasyāḥ kukṣiṁ gataḥ kṛṣṇo dvitīyo vibudhaiḥ stutaḥ “Kṛṣṇa appeared in the womb of Devakī after transferring Baladeva to the womb of Rohiṇī by the power of Yoga-māyā.” Yadubhiḥ sa vyarudhyata. The kings of the Yadu dynasty were all devotees, but there were many powerful demons, such as Śālva, who began to persecute them. At that time, Jarāsandha, who was Kaṁsa’s father-in-law, was extremely powerful, and therefore Kaṁsa took advantage of his protection and the help of the demons in persecuting the kings of the Yadu dynasty. The demons naturally appeared more powerful than the demigods, but ultimately, because of help received from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the demons were defeated and the demigods triumphant.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Under the protection of Magadharāja, Jarāsandha, the powerful Kaṁsa began persecuting the kings of the Yadu dynasty. In this he had the cooperation of demons like Pralamba, Baka, Cāṇūra, Tṛṇāvarta, Aghāsura, Muṣṭika, Ariṣṭa, Dvivida, Pūtanā, Keśī, Dhenuka, Bāṇāsura, Narakāsura and many other demoniac kings on the surface of the earth.
    Commentary

    In the second chapter the child of Devaki is transferred to Rohini by Yogamaya, Krsna appears in Devaki’s womb and the devatas praise the Lord. Kamsa’s persecution of the Yadus, which was mentioned in the first chapter, is now described in detail. In this list of the asuras, Mahasana (big eater) means Aghasura.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The kings gathered together because of the protection of Jarāsandha.

    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    When demoniac power overwhelms the world, Kṛṣṇa Himself descends to protect His devotees and restore dharma — never doubt His personal intervention.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where adharma is pressing on you or those you serve, and respond by taking explicit shelter of Kṛṣṇa rather than relying on your own strength.
    • Speak Kṛṣṇa's name aloud at least once when you feel surrounded by 'demons' — distractions, hostile people, or inner asuric tendencies — and trust His paritrāṇāya promise.
    • Refuse the cynical view that the world is hopeless; remember that the Yadus, though persecuted, were never abandoned, and serve someone today as if protecting a devotee under siege.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I, like Kaṁsa, taking shelter of a 'Jarāsandha' — some powerful worldly alliance, ideology, or institution — to legitimize a course of action I already sense is opposed to Kṛṣṇa's purpose?
    • When I see the demonic forces of this age seeming to overpower the devotees and the dharmic, do I quietly conclude that adharma is winning — and what does that quiet conclusion reveal about how much I actually trust paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Identify one 'Kaṁsa' in your social media feed — an account or trend that quietly persecutes your sādhana (your study, your sleep, your self-respect). This week, name its 'Jarāsandha' (the algorithm, the friend group, the FOMO) and cut one specific tie, not vaguely 'use less phone.'
    • In your friend group there is almost always a person who plays Kaṁsa's role — mocking sincerity, pressuring everyone toward viṣaya. Without becoming self-righteous, decide today what you will not laugh along with anymore. Write the line in your notes app.
    • Before your next exam or deadline, do the Yadu-practice: act with full effort while internally taking shelter of Kṛṣṇa. Notice the difference between anxious striving (you alone against Kaṁsa) and śaraṇāgata striving (you working, He arranging).
    householder
    • Audit one area of family life — schooling, finances, in-laws, screen time — where an adharmic pattern persists because a 'Jarāsandha' protects it (a relative's pressure, a job's demands, a school's culture). Name it aloud with your spouse this week and decide together on one concrete withdrawal.
    • When you face a workplace 'Kaṁsa' — a boss or client who persecutes the honest path — practice the Yadu posture: do not flatter, do not flee, keep doing your duty, and inwardly hand the outcome to Kṛṣṇa. Each evening, formally offer the day's frictions to Him.
    • Teach your children the difference between real karuṇā (serving the soul) and material compassion (only easing the body). Do this not by lecture but by one visible decision this month — saying no to something they want because it harms their long-term dharma.
    senior
    • You have lived through several cycles of 'Kaṁsas' — political, professional, familial — and seen the Lord's rearrangements unfold. Tell one such story this week to a younger person, not as nostalgia but as evidence: glānir bhavati, then sambhavāmi. Make the Gītā 4.7-8 pattern concrete for them.
    • Examine the attachments you are still defending as 'protecting the family' — properties, control of decisions, opinions about how things should go. Ask honestly: am I a Yadu taking shelter, or have I quietly become a small Jarāsandha sheltering someone else's Kaṁsa? Loosen one grip this month.
    • As mortality nears, the demons of fear, regret, and bodily decline grow louder. Do not fight them on their terms. Instead, deepen one act of śaraṇāgati daily — japa, hearing SB, remembering Kṛṣṇa's names — trusting that He who appears 'yuge yuge' also appears at the hour of a devotee's passage.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the long list of demons as mere mythology or distant history, rather than recognizing the same Pralamba-Baka-Pūtanā impulses (illusion, deceit, false nourishment, distraction) operating inside one's own ahaṅkāra today.
    • Mistaking the demons' apparent supremacy for actual strength — concluding that aligning with worldly power (the 'Jarāsandha shelter') is pragmatic, when the verse's whole arc shows such shelter guarantees eventual destruction by the Lord Himself.
    • Twisting 'vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām' into a license for personal vindictiveness or political crusading against people one labels 'demonic,' rather than seeing it as Kṛṣṇa's prerogative and turning the same scrutiny inward on one's own duṣkṛta tendencies.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa did not act alone — Jarāsandha sheltered him, and a roster of demons cooperated. In your own life, name one adharmic pattern you participate in that depends on a 'Jarāsandha' (an institution, friend, or system that protects it). Would you actually withdraw that protection? Disagree honestly with each other about whether withdrawal is realistic.
    • Prabhupāda says political leaders 'try to hinder the purpose of the Lord.' Pair up and argue both sides: is it ever genuine devotional service to engage with politics and worldly power for the sake of dharma, or does that engagement always corrupt? Bring concrete present-day examples.
    • The verse names many demons by name — Pūtanā, Tṛṇāvarta, Aghāsura, and so on. Why does Śukadeva bother with the catalogue rather than saying 'and many demons'? In your group, propose competing answers (memorial, literary, devotional, strategic) and see if you can agree which is primary.
    Role Play

    A teacher divides the class into three roles. One student plays a devoted Yadu citizen whose family business has just been seized by Kaṁsa's tax-collectors. A second plays their cousin, who counsels patience — 'Kṛṣṇa will appear in His own time; do not provoke Kaṁsa.' A third plays a hot-headed neighbor urging armed resistance now. Run the scene for ten minutes. Then debrief: where in the conversation did real karuṇā speak, and where did rajas masquerade as it? What would saraṇāgati look like for each character today, before Kṛṣṇa's appearance is visible?

    Objections & Responses
    • Calling political opponents 'demons' is exactly the kind of dehumanizing rhetoric that has fueled real-world violence. Isn't this verse just sanctifying us-versus-them thinking?
      A fair worry, and worth taking seriously. But notice what the text actually does: it names asuras by their conduct — persecuting devotees, obstructing the Lord's purpose — not by birth, ethnicity, or party. Kaṁsa himself was a Yadu by blood; Jarāsandha was a respected king. The category is moral and behavioral, not tribal. Further, the Gauḍīya teacher never authorizes us to play Kṛṣṇa's role of 'vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām.' Our work is sādhana and bhakti; annihilating miscreants is His prerogative, not ours. The verse trains us to see clearly, not to swing swords.
    • If Kṛṣṇa is supreme and protects His devotees, why were the Yadus — His own family — being persecuted in the first place? Either He isn't fully in control, or He doesn't really protect His own.
      Both horns of the dilemma assume that protection means absence of difficulty. But Prabhupāda's purport quotes BG 4.7-8 to frame the persecution as the very stage on which the Lord descends. The Yadus' suffering is not a failure of Kṛṣṇa's protection; it is the invitation for Kṛṣṇa's appearance. A devotee learns to read distress as the front edge of the Lord's intervention rather than as His absence. This is also why the Gauḍīyas treasure verses like BG 12.5 — the personal Lord meets His devotees inside their actual conditions, He does not airlift them out of history.

    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Persecuted by the demoniac kings, the Yādavas left their own kingdom and entered various others, like those of the Kurus, Paṣcālas, Kekayas, Śālvas, Vidarbhas, Niṣadhas, Videhas and Kośalas.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The Yadus lived in secret (nibhṛtam viviśuḥ), hiding in farming and cowherd villages dressed in farmers’ or cowherds’ clothing.

    Related values & verses
    Related verses
    SB 10.2.1 SB 10.2.4 SB 10.2.6
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Even Kṛṣṇa's own Yādavas were driven from their homeland — devotional life does not exempt you from upheaval; it teaches you to take shelter through it.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you expect bhakti to remove difficulty rather than steady you within it, and correct that expectation in your morning sādhana.
    • When forced out of a comfortable situation — a role, a city, a relationship — refuse to read it as Kṛṣṇa's absence; treat the displacement itself as His arrangement.
    • Speak to one person who has been uprooted (a relocated colleague, a struggling family member) and offer concrete shelter — a meal, a call, a place to sit — as a small Yādava-like refuge.
    Reflection Questions
    • When my own 'kingdom' — my routine, my settled life — is disturbed by hostile pressure, do I read it as senseless persecution, or am I willing to consider it as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement to relocate me toward where He wants me?
    • Like the Yādavas scattered among the Kurus, Pañcālas, and Kośalas, where in my life am I being asked to live among people who do not share my values, and how am I preserving my devotional identity inside that exile?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When your friend group, your hostel, or your campus turns hostile to your sādhana — chanting mocked, vegetarianism teased, your morning program treated as weird — do not flatten yourself to fit in. Identify one 'Kuru' or 'Pañcāla' in your life: a single devotee friend, an online sangha, a teacher, a senior — and physically go there (a call, a visit, a meeting) this week. The Yādavas did not survive by toughing it out alone; they survived by entering somebody's kingdom.
    • Notice the social-media equivalent of being 'persecuted by demoniac kings' — the algorithm pushing viṣaya at you all day. Do not pretend you are above it. Today, deliberately migrate: unfollow three accounts that erode your sādhana and follow three that feed it. This is not aesthetic curation; it is the same act the Yādavas performed when they crossed a border.
    • Before your next exam or placement interview, separate the dhīra question from the panic question. The panic question is 'will I get the result I want?' The dhīra question is 'am I doing the work Kṛṣṇa has placed in front of me with full attention?' Write both questions on paper, answer only the second one, and offer the first to Him.
    householder
    • The Yādavas had to move their families — wives, children, elders — under pressure. When your family faces a forced transition (a job loss, a relocation, a school change, a parent's illness), do not perform false steadiness for the kids. Sit with your spouse, name the pressure honestly, and then make one Kṛṣṇa-conscious decision together this week — where to go for shelter, whom to lean on, what to let go of. The verse models that displacement is a family decision, not a private one.
    • Audit the 'kingdoms' you currently shelter in: the school district, the workplace, the neighborhood, the in-laws' house. Which ones are Kuru-level (genuinely supportive of your family's bhakti) and which are demoniac-king-level (slowly eroding it)? You do not have to flee tomorrow, but make one concrete adjustment this month — a different school activity, a different social circle for the kids, a different commute that frees up a chanting window.
    • When money pressure or career pressure makes you want to compromise on a principle (cutting corners at work, taking on debt for status, skipping your offering to save time), remember: the Yādavas left their kingdom rather than betray their dharma. Identify one place this week where you have been quietly negotiating with your own conscience and stop the negotiation. Lose the kingdom, keep the sva-dharma.
    senior
    • The Yādavas had to leave behind built lives — homes, fields, positions — because the time had come. At your stage, the 'demoniac kings' are not external persecutors; they are the body itself, the slow eviction notice. Identify one attachment this month — a possession, a role, an authority you still cling to — and consciously hand it to a younger person. Practice the migration before it is forced.
    • You are now in a position to be a 'Kuru' or a 'Vidarbha' for displaced devotees — younger people whose families do not support their bhakti, householders in crisis, students far from home. Open your house, your phone, or your kitchen to one such person this month. Mentoring at this age is not optional charity; it is the dharma of being the established kingdom that takes others in.
    • Speak about death in plain language with your spouse and children — not as morbid preparation but as the natural next migration. Tell them concretely: where you want your remaining years spent, what you want done with what you leave behind, and most importantly, what you want them to remember about Kṛṣṇa when you go. The dhīra does not pretend the body's transition is not coming; he names it, settles it, and returns to chanting.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Romanticizing the Yādavas' exile as a passive 'trust the process' lesson, while ignoring that they were actively protecting Kṛṣṇa's appearance — misapplied as an excuse for fatalism instead of vigilant action.
    • Reading the verse as merely historical geography (Kuru, Pañcāla, Kekaya, etc.) and skipping the inner application — that the devotee's circumstances are arranged around Kṛṣṇa's mission, not around personal comfort.
    • Treating persecution by 'demoniac kings' as a license to label every difficult person in one's life as a demon, breeding paranoia and self-righteousness instead of sober discernment and dependence on Kṛṣṇa.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The Yādavas — Kṛṣṇa's own kinsmen, devotees of the Lord — are forced to flee and scatter into foreign kingdoms. If even those closest to Kṛṣṇa face displacement and persecution, what does that say about the promises we tell ourselves that bhakti will make life materially smooth? Where in your own life have you secretly bargained with Kṛṣṇa: 'I will surrender, but please keep my situation stable'?
    • When the Yādavas entered Kuru, Pañcāla, Kekaya and the rest, they remained Yādavas — Kṛṣṇa's people — even in exile. Share a time when you had to keep your sādhana alive in a place that was not built for it (a hostile workplace, a non-devotee household, a foreign city). Did you compromise to fit in, or did you let the surroundings reshape you? Where do you still disagree with the group on what 'adjustment' versus 'capitulation' looks like?
    • The verse names eight specific kingdoms — these are not interchangeable backdrops; they are real shelters given by real people. Who in your life has been a Kuru or a Vidarbha for you — someone who took you in when you were under pressure? And who have you refused to shelter because it was inconvenient? Disagree honestly: is sheltering devotees a duty, a luxury, or a privilege?
    Role Play

    Two students play a married Yādava couple who have just fled Mathurā with their small children and what little they could carry. They arrive at the gate of a Pañcāla family — played by two other students — who are devotees but already stretched thin (limited rooms, school-age kids of their own, a fixed income). The Yādavas must ask for shelter without manipulating; the Pañcālas must respond without performing generosity they cannot sustain. Run the scene twice — once where the host says yes with conditions, once where the host says no with care — and then debrief: which response was more truly compassionate in the Gauḍīya sense (serving the soul), and which was material compassion (avoiding awkwardness)? What did Kṛṣṇa-consciousness actually require of each party?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Personality of Godhead and the Yādavas are His own dynasty, why does He let them be 'persecuted by demoniac kings' at all? A loving God who couldn't or wouldn't protect His own family looks either weak or cruel. This whole verse is an embarrassment for the personalist position.
      The verse is not an embarrassment; it is the answer. Kṛṣṇa's protection of His devotees is never the protection of their material arrangements — it is the protection of their bhakti. By scattering the Yādavas into Kuru, Pañcāla, Vidarbha and the rest, He is doing two things at once: ripening the karmic accounts of the demoniac kings (which is its own mercy on them) and seeding devotee-culture across the subcontinent so that when He appears in Mathurā, the ground is already prepared. A 'loving God' who simply kept His devotees comfortable would be the God of material compassion — the very thing the Gītā opens by rejecting. Kṛṣṇa's love is the love that serves the soul, which sometimes looks, from the outside, like displacement.
    • This is a list of ancient kingdom names that mean nothing to a modern reader. We're not in Vidarbha. We're not Yādavas. Why am I supposed to find personal guidance in what is essentially a refugee migration map from three thousand years ago?
      The Bhāgavatam never wastes a verse on geography for its own sake. The eight names are the point: persecution does not produce one response, it produces eight — each Yādava family had to discern where to go, whom to trust, what to carry, what to leave. That discernment under pressure is exactly what your life asks of you. Whenever you are pushed out of a comfortable arrangement — a job ends, a relationship breaks, a city becomes unlivable, a community turns — you are doing what the Yādavas did. The verse is not asking you to identify with a tribe; it is asking you to notice that even Kṛṣṇa's own people were given the dignity of having to choose their next shelter, and so are you. The diacritics on 'Vidarbhān' matter precisely because the specifics matter — yours do too.

    Some of their relatives, however, began to follow Kaṁsa’s principles and act in his service. After Kaṁsa, the son of Ugrasena, killed the six sons of Devakī, a plenary portion of Kṛṣṇa entered her womb as her seventh child, arousing her pleasure and her lamentation. That plenary portion is celebrated by great sages as Ananta, who belongs to Kṛṣṇa’s second quadruple expansion.
    Purport

    Some of the chief devotees, such as Akrūra, stayed with Kaṁsa to satisfy him. This they did for various purposes. They all expected the Supreme Personality of Godhead to appear as the eighth child as soon as Devakī’s other children were killed by Kaṁsa, and they were eagerly awaiting His appearance. By remaining in Kaṁsa’s association, they would be able to see the Supreme Personality of Godhead take birth and display His childhood pastimes, and Akrūra would later go to Vṛndāvana to bring Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā. The word paryupāsate is significant because it indicates that some devotees wanted to stay near Kaṁsa in order to see all these pastimes of the Lord. The six children killed by Kaṁsa had formerly been sons of Marīci, but because of having been cursed by a brāhmaṇa, they were obliged to take birth as grandsons of Hiraṇyakaśipu. Kaṁsa had taken birth as Kālanemi, and now he was obliged to kill his own sons. This was a mystery. As soon as the sons of Devakī were killed, they would return to their original place. The devotees wanted to see this also. Generally speaking, no one kills his own nephews, but Kaṁsa was so cruel that he did so without hesitation. Ananta, Saṅkarṣaṇa, belongs to the second catur-vyūha, or quadruple expansion. This is the opinion of experienced commentators.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Some of their relatives, however, began to follow Kaṁsa's principles and act in his service. After Kaṁsa, the son of Ugrasena, killed the six sons of Devakī, a plenary portion of Kṛṣṇa entered her womb as her seventh child, arousing her pleasure and her lamentation. That plenary portion is celebrated by great sages as Ananta, who belongs to Kṛṣṇa's second quadruple expansion.
    Commentary

    Being eager to see the Lord, some of the Yadus such as Akrura became cooperative with Kamsa and lived with him in Mathura. After Kamsa killed the first six children, the seventh appeared in Devaki’s womb. He is famous as Ananta. What is his description? He is described as vaisnava dhama, That means an amsa of Krsna. That he appeared in the womb was a cause of jubilation, but that he would be killed by Kamsa was a cause of lamentation.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Some of the Yadus’ relatives followed Kaṁsa. This means that they skillfully were able to control him. Or, some devotees did this because they were waiting to see Kṛṣṇa. This will later be revealed by Akrūra when he goes to Vraja. Paryupāsate should be paryupāsata. The six children who were killed were previously devatā sons of Marīci but by offending Brahmā they became demons. They were born to Kālanemi, son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, as his six sons known as the ṣaḍ-garbha. Rejecting Hiraṇyakaśipu they began worshipping Brahmā. Angry at that, Hiraṇyakaśipu cursed them to be killed by their father. Remembering this incident, the Lord had Yogamāyā put them in the womb of Devakī, to be killed by Kaṁsa, who was previously their father Kālameni. This is explained in Hari-vamśa. Later it will be said that they appeared from Hiraṇyakaśipu (hiraṇyakaśipor jātā nītās te yoga-māyayā ( SB 10.85.48). To harmonize the two statements, the meaning should be that they were born as Kālameni’s sons, in Hiraṇyakaśipu’s lineage. Thus in the later verse it is simply stated they appeared (jātāḥ) from Hiraṇyakaśipu, and that does not mention they were his sons. This is also stated in Mahābhārata. Or, there can be different versions in different kalpas. Though they were killed, it is explained in Chapter Eighty-five that they attained liberation from hellish condition. Thus no one can accuse the Lord of being indifferent to their killing. Because of his anger Śukadeva does not mention Kaṁsa’s name but instead calls him “son of Ugrasena.” The wise call the seventh child Saṅkarṣaṇa (anantam), the second member of the caturvyūha, whose body was filled with Kṛṣṇa (vaiṣṇavam).

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Daksya (Resourcefulness / Skill)Adambhitva (Non-hypocrisy / Authenticity)Discriminative Wisdom
    Related verses
    SB 10.2.1 SB 10.2.3 SB 10.2.6 SB 10.2.7 BG 9.11 BG 15.2 BG 6.1 BG 6.47 BG 5.4 BG 9.1
    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Even amid Kaṁsa's tyranny, devotees stay close to witness Kṛṣṇa's pastimes — the Lord arranges every cruelty and joy to set the stage for His appearance.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one situation today where you've labeled circumstances 'bad' and ask what pastime of Kṛṣṇa they may be setting the stage for.
    • Like Akrūra remaining near Kaṁsa, stay engaged in your difficult post today rather than fleeing — serve with the inner aim of seeing Kṛṣṇa act through it.
    • Refuse the impulse to resolve every harṣa-śoka swing in your day; sit with both pleasure and lamentation as Devakī did, awaiting the Lord within.
    Reflection Questions
    • Like Akrūra remaining in Kaṁsa's court to witness Kṛṣṇa's appearance, where am I being asked to stay inside an uncomfortable or compromising situation — not to serve it, but to be present for the Lord's work that will unfold there?
    • Devakī's womb carried both harṣa and śoka simultaneously when Ananta entered — where in my own life am I refusing to hold joy and lamentation together, demanding that surrender feel like only one or the other?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Identify the 'Kaṁsa-court' in your life right now — the friend group, the group chat, the campus scene whose values you actually disagree with. Are you there as Akrūra (present with a clear devotional purpose) or just because leaving is socially expensive? Write down which one, honestly, this week.
    • Devakī carried both joy and grief in the same pregnancy. Next time a result comes in — an exam grade, an internship rejection, a like-count on a post — practice holding the swing without immediately posting, venting, or numbing. Sit with the harṣa-śoka for ten minutes and offer it.
    • The six previous sons had been cursed and were working off karma through Kaṁsa's hand — a hidden order behind apparent injustice. When something feels unfair this semester (a grade, a breakup, being left out), resist the impulse to immediately narrate yourself as victim. Ask instead: what is being burned off here, and what is being prepared?
    householder
    • You almost certainly work or live inside at least one 'Kaṁsa-system' — a workplace, an industry, an extended-family dynamic whose values are not yours. Apply Akrūra's three tests this month: is there a specific service only you can render here, is your inner alignment intact, and are you actually ready to act when the moment comes? If not all three, plan your exit; if yes, stay with explicit intent.
    • Devakī's joy-and-grief is the householder's daily condition — the same child who delights you also exposes your selfishness; the same career that funds your sādhana also drains it. Stop trying to resolve that tension into pure joy. Each evening, name one harṣa and one śoka of the day and offer both to Kṛṣṇa, the way Devakī carried both at once.
    • When raising your children, do not flatten the spiritual story into 'be nice.' Tell them about Kaṁsa, about Devakī's loss, about Akrūra's strange patience — let them inherit a tradition with real moral weight, not a sanitized version that will not survive their first contact with adult cruelty.
    senior
    • Akrūra waited years inside Kaṁsa's court for one specific act of service — bringing Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma to Mathurā. In this season of life, identify the one or two acts of service that may be the real reason you are still here, and stop scattering your energies. The rest is paryupāsate — sitting near, ready.
    • Devakī lost six children before the seventh was even conceived. You have likely lost more than you expected by now — friends, parents, capacities, perhaps a child. The tradition does not ask you to call that loss good; it asks you to carry harṣa and śoka together, as she did, without letting either calcify into bitterness or denial. Practice this in your daily remembrance.
    • Mentor a younger householder or youth this year specifically on the difference between real compassion (serving the soul) and material compassion (smoothing over bodily discomfort). Your age gives you authority on this that no one in their twenties has. Do not waste it on generic advice — give them the Gītā's pivot, in your own words, from your own losses.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Akrūra's outward service to Kaṁsa as license to stay entangled in any compromising association — forgetting that his presence there was specifically Kṛṣṇa-conscious, purposeful, and temporary, not a justification for ordinary attachment.
    • Treating the killing of Devakī's six sons as mere narrative cruelty and missing the deeper teaching — that what looks like loss in this world is often the soul returning to its original position, which only the devotee's vision can perceive.
    • Conflating Ananta-Saṅkarṣaṇa with Kṛṣṇa Himself, or dismissing Him as a 'lesser' expansion — both errors collapse the personal, hierarchical structure of the catur-vyūha into either impersonalism or demigod-worship.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Akrūra and other devotees stayed inside Kaṁsa's court — eating his food, attending his meetings — purely to be near where Kṛṣṇa would appear. Where in your own life are you tolerating an environment you find distasteful because the spiritual payoff is real, and where are you just rationalizing comfort? Push each other on the difference.
    • Devakī's seventh pregnancy is described as harṣa-śoka-vivardhanaḥ — simultaneously increasing her joy and her lamentation. Share a recent situation where bhakti has produced both feelings in you at once. Does the modern instinct to 'resolve' that tension actually serve the soul, or does Devakī's example suggest something else?
    • The verse says 'some' relatives followed Kaṁsa's principles to serve him — implying others did not, and were presumably killed or exiled. If you had been in that family, which group would you honestly have joined, and on what grounds? Don't let each other off with the pious answer.
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a devotee working at a tech company whose product they've come to believe is harming users (think social media engagement traps). They are considering quitting on principle. Student B is an older Vaiṣṇava friend who points out that Akrūra stayed in Kaṁsa's court — not to enjoy it, but because the Lord's work required someone to be positioned there. Student B argues for staying with paryupāsate-like intent: present, internally non-aligned, awaiting the moment of useful service. Student A must distinguish this from self-deceiving rationalization. Run the conversation for ten minutes; then swap and run it again with the roles reversed. Debrief: what tests would you apply to know which side of that line you are actually on?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole story is mythological — a tyrant king killing infants because of a prophecy, a 'plenary portion' descending into a womb. Why are we extracting life-guidance from a fairy tale instead of just naming the moral (don't be cruel) and moving on?
      The Bhāgavatam is not asking you to believe a fairy tale; it is presenting Kṛṣṇa-līlā as the deepest layer of reality, recorded by liberated sages. But even if a skeptic brackets the metaphysics, notice what gets lost by reducing the verse to 'don't be cruel': you lose Akrūra's strategic patience inside an evil court, you lose Devakī's harṣa-śoka as a model for devotion under pressure, you lose Ananta as the second catur-vyūha — the structural fact that Kṛṣṇa's expansions precede and prepare His appearance. The 'just take the moral' approach is precisely the impersonalist drift the tradition warns against. We hold the personal Kṛṣṇa, His pastimes, and His devotees as real — and only then do the practical lessons land with weight.
    • The devotees stayed near Kaṁsa to 'see the pastimes.' Isn't that just spiritual voyeurism — proximity to power dressed up as devotion? Plenty of people today justify staying in toxic systems by saying they're 'doing God's work from inside.'
      A fair pushback, and the tradition itself names the test. Akrūra's staying was paryupāsate — sitting near with worshipful intent, awaiting a specific service that only he could render (later, going to Vṛndāvana to bring Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma). Three marks distinguish him from the modern rationalizer. First, the service was assigned by the situation, not chosen for prestige — he was not enjoying Kaṁsa's wealth. Second, his internal alignment never shifted — he never began defending Kaṁsa, only enduring him. Third, when the moment of real service came, he acted, even at risk. Apply those three tests to anyone (including yourself) claiming to do God's work from inside a Kaṁsa-court. If the service is vague, the alignment has drifted, and the moment of action keeps getting postponed — it is voyeurism, or worse, complicity. Bhakti is exacting on this point.

    To protect the Yadus, His personal devotees, from Kaṁsa’s attack, the Personality of Godhead, Viśvātmā, the Supreme Soul of everyone, ordered Yoga-māyā as follows.
    Purport

    The words bhagavān api viśvātmā viditvā kaṁsajaṁ bhayam are commented upon by Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī. Bhagavān svayam is Kṛṣṇa ( kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam ). He is Viśvātmā, the original Supersoul of everyone, because His plenary portion expands as the Supersoul. This is confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā (13.3) : kṣetra-jñaṁ cāpi māṁ viddhi sarva-kṣetreṣu bhārata. Lord Kṛṣṇa is the kṣetra jña, or Supersoul, of all living entities. He is the original source of all expansions of the Personality of Godhead. There are hundreds and thousands of plenary expansions of Viṣṇu, such as Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha and Vāsudeva, but here in this material world, the Viśvātmā, the Supersoul for all living entities, is Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (18.61) , īśvaraḥ sarva-bhūtānāṁ hṛd-deśe ’rjuna tiṣṭhati: “The Supreme Lord is situated in the heart of all living entities, O Arjuna.” Kṛṣṇa is actually Viśvātmā by His plenary expansion as viṣṇu-tattva, yet because of His affection for His devotees, He acts as Supersoul to give them directions ( sarvasya cāhaṁ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo mattaḥ smṛtir jñānam apohanaṁ ca ). The affairs of the Supersoul pertain to Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu, but Kṛṣṇa took compassion on Devakī, His devotee, because He understood her fear of Kaṁsa’s persecution. A pure devotee is always fearful of material existence. No one knows what will happen next, for one may have to change his body at any moment ( tathā dehāntara-prāptiḥ ). Knowing this fact, a pure devotee acts in such a way that he will not have his life spoiled by being obliged to accept another body and undergo the tribulations of material existence. This is bhayam, or fear. Bhayaṁ dvitīyābhiniveśataḥ syāt ( Bhāg. 11.2.37 ). This fear is due to material existence. Properly speaking, everyone should always be alert and fearful of material existence, but although everyone is prone to be affected by the ignorance of material existence, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, is always alert to the protection of His devotees. Kṛṣṇa is so kind and affectionate toward His devotees that He helps them by giving them the intelligence by which to exist in this material world without forgetting Him even for a moment. The Lord says: teṣām evānukampārtham aham ajñāna-jaṁ tamaḥ nāśayāmy ātma-bhāvastho jñāna-dīpena bhāsvatā “Out of compassion for them, I, dwelling in their hearts, destroy with the shining lamp of knowledge the darkness born of ignorance.” ( Bg. 10.11 ) The word yoga means “link.” Any system of yoga is an attempt to reconnect our broken relationship with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. There are different types of yoga, of which bhakti-yoga is the best. In other yoga systems, one must undergo various processes before attaining perfection, but bhakti-yoga is direct. The Lord says in Bhagavad-gītā (6.47) : yoginām api sarveṣāṁ mad-gatenāntarātmanā śraddhāvān bhajate yo māṁ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ “Of all yogīs, he who always abides in Me with great faith, worshiping Me in transcendental loving service, is most intimately united with Me in yoga and is the highest of all.” For the bhakti-yogī, a human body is guaranteed in his next existence, as stated by Lord Kṛṣṇa ( śucīnāṁ śrīmatāṁ gehe yoga-bhraṣṭo ’bhijāyate ). Yoga-māyā is the spiritual potency of the Lord. Out of affection for His devotees, the Lord always stays in spiritual touch with them, although otherwise His Māyā potency is so strong that she bewilders even exalted demigods like Brahmā. Therefore the Lord’s potency is called Yoga-māyā. Since the Lord is Viśvātmā, He immediately ordered Yoga-māyā to give protection to Devakī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    To protect the Yadus, His personal devotees, from Kaṁsa's attack, the Personality of Godhead, Viśvātmā, the Supreme Soul of everyone, ordered Yogamāyā as follows.
    Commentary

    Krsna, svayam bhagavan, gave orders to Yogamaya, who is the fifth of his nine spiritual energies headed by Vimala.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Svayam Bhagavān, Kṛṣṇa, the aṁśī of all forms of God (viśvātmā), knew that the Yadus feared Kaṁsa. The word api is used to distinguish Kṛṣṇa who speaks at this time from Kṣīrodakaśāyī (who is his aṁśa) who spoke to Brahmā previously. He knew of their suffering without having to be informed of it. Therefore he spoke to Yogamāyā to relieve the Yadus of fear. He ordered her in a stimulating way (samyak ādiśat). Why? They took refuge in him alone (nija-nāthānām). Therefore out of affection for them he did this. Or the phrase can mean that they were the best (nāthānām) of all his devotees (nija). Yoga means a special śakti of the Lord and it is called māyā because it has the ability of bewilder even Brahmā. It is superior to the śakti which causes the material universe (jagat-kāraṇa-śakti). Another name of Yogamāyā is Ekānaṁśā. Another meaning of the sentence by interpreting the word api is that it indicates the supreme position of Bhagavān in comparison with māyā. Since he was in the supreme position he ordered Yogamāyā.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word api is used to distinguish Kṛṣṇa, who speaks at this time, from Kṣīrodakaśāyī (who is his aṁśa) who spoke to Brahmā previously. He knew because he was all pervading (viśvātmā). Or knowing the Yadu’s fear because he was antaryāmī, he acted to destroy their fear without being asked. He ordered Yogamāyā in a stimulating way (sam ādiśat). Why? The lords of the Yadus were his relatives (nija-nāthānām). He was affectionate to his devotees. Or because he was the lord (viśvātmā), he gave orders to Yogamāyā, who was dependent on him. Yoga means a special śakti of the Lord. It is called māyā because it can bewilder even Brahmā.

    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa, Viśvātmā, dispatches Yoga-māyā to shield His devotees — surrender keeps you inside the circle of His personal protection.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one fear of material existence (bhayam) you carry today, and hand it to Kṛṣṇa in your morning prayer instead of carrying it alone.
    • Refuse the impersonalist drift: address Kṛṣṇa by name when you chant or pray today, not 'the universe' or 'the Self'.
    • Notice one moment today when intelligence arises to keep you from forgetting Him — thank Him for it as the Supersoul's direct help.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life have I been trying to protect myself through my own arrangements, instead of crying out to Kṛṣṇa as Devakī did and trusting that He will dispatch Yoga-māyā on my behalf?
    • What 'Kaṁsa' am I refusing to name as a real fear — the next forced change of body, situation, or relationship — and how has my refusal to face it kept me from sincere shelter-taking?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When exam season or a friend-group betrayal triggers panic, name it as bhayam — fear born of identifying with the temporary body and its situation — and chant Hare Kṛṣṇa for ten minutes before opening any social media. Test whether the shaking actually subsides; do not take it on faith.
    • Pick one peer you secretly compete with and, for one week, treat them as another spark of the same Viśvātmā that lives in you — text them a genuine note when they win something. Notice what dies in you (ahaṅkāra) and what stays (you).
    • On Instagram you are constantly invited to perform a 'self' to be protected by likes. Devakī's protection came from yoga-māyā, not from posting her crisis. For one week, do not post anything about your inner life — bring those things instead to your japa and to one trusted devotee. Watch whether your interior gets stronger or weaker.
    householder
    • Your kids and spouse are not yours; they are souls Kṛṣṇa has placed in your care, the way Devakī was placed under Yoga-māyā's protection. Once a week, before a major family decision (school, money, move), explicitly pray: 'Kṛṣṇa, You are Viśvātmā in their hearts too — guide me to serve, not to control.' Then act, and release the result.
    • The Kaṁsa in a householder's life is usually financial fear — job loss, market crash, kids' education costs. When it grips you, recall bhayaṁ dvitīyābhiniveśataḥ syāt: this fear is structural to material existence, not a sign you have failed. Do the next concrete responsible action (update the resume, call the advisor) and offer the outcome to Kṛṣṇa at your evening sādhana. Refuse to let the fear extend past the work it is meant to fuel.
    • Make your home a place where Yoga-māyā can act: install regular family kīrtana, prasāda, and reading — even fifteen minutes daily. Children raised in this atmosphere are protected in ways no school district or savings account can match, because Kṛṣṇa Himself takes interest in homes that take interest in Him.
    senior
    • At 60+ you have already 'transitioned through' infant, child, youth, householder bodies — the soul is unchanged, as the dhīra knows. Sit each morning and feel that continuity; let it weaken your grip on this current body's preferences (food, comfort, routine) one notch at a time.
    • Kṛṣṇa protected Devakī because she was His devotee; the protection you most need now is not from illness or loneliness but from forgetting Him at the moment of death (ante nārāyaṇa-smṛtiḥ). Reorganize your day so that japa, hearing Bhāgavatam, and the holy name are the spine — and meals, errands, and even family calls are arranged around that spine, not the reverse.
    • Your real legacy is not the inheritance, the photo albums, or the stories — it is the bhakti you transmit. Identify one younger person (grandchild, neighbor, junior colleague) and, without preaching, share one verse, one prasādam meal, one kīrtana evening per month. Yoga-māyā can use even a small offering through a sincere elder to plant a seed that protects a soul for lifetimes.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Yoga-māyā as an impersonal force or 'cosmic energy' rather than the Lord's personal spiritual potency, dispatched by Kṛṣṇa Himself out of affection for His devotees.
    • Concluding that because Kṛṣṇa is Viśvātmā in everyone's heart, He is equally close to all — and therefore neglecting the specific intimacy He reserves for surrendered devotees like Devakī, who actually receive His protective intervention.
    • Misreading the verse's bhayam as worldly anxiety to be soothed away, when Prabhupāda explicitly says a pure devotee should remain alert and fearful of material existence (bhayaṁ dvitīyābhiniveśataḥ syāt) — the cure is shelter in Kṛṣṇa, not the elimination of vigilance.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda says a pure devotee is 'always fearful of material existence' (bhayaṁ dvitīyābhiniveśataḥ syāt), yet Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna 'do not fear.' Pair up: where does each of you draw the line between healthy bhaya of material existence and faithless anxiety? Push back on each other when one of you collapses the distinction.
    • Kṛṣṇa, who is Viśvātmā for everyone, takes special action to protect Devakī because she is His devotee. Discuss in threes: does this make Kṛṣṇa 'partial'? Is impartiality even a virtue in a personal relationship with God, or is it a borrowed Enlightenment idea we should drop?
    • The purport says bhakti-yoga is 'direct' while other yogas require many preliminary processes. In your group, name one 'preliminary process' (study, meditation technique, ethical self-improvement) you have been treating as the main thing. Are you willing to demote it to the role of supporter of bhakti, or do you secretly think it is more reliable than chanting and hearing? Be honest with each other.
    Role Play

    Two students play out this scene: A is a devotee whose elderly mother has just been diagnosed with a serious illness. A's faith is shaken — 'If Kṛṣṇa protects His devotees, why is she suffering? Devakī got Yoga-māyā; what do we get?' B is a slightly more senior devotee in the same congregation who must respond — without platitudes, without denying A's grief, and without abandoning the verse's claim that Kṛṣṇa actively protects His devotees. B must distinguish material protection (the body) from real protection (the soul's progress and remembrance of Kṛṣṇa at the time of death), and must do so while sitting with A in real distress, not lecturing. After 5 minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did B slip into either cold theology or sentimental reassurance?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just mythological favoritism. A 'Supreme Soul of everyone' who then plays favorites for His 'personal devotees' is a contradiction — and morally suspect. Why should I trust a God who allegedly loves all but acts only for some?
      The contradiction dissolves once you see that Kṛṣṇa is Viśvātmā by His plenary expansion as Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu — He is impartially present in every heart, giving everyone the intelligence and remembrance their karma allows (sarvasya cāhaṁ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo). What changes for the devotee is not Kṛṣṇa's availability but the devotee's reciprocation. Yoga-māyā is dispatched not because Devakī earned a prize but because she has turned toward Him in love, and love by its nature responds personally. The sun shines on every field; only the field that has been ploughed and seeded yields a crop. To call this 'favoritism' is to demand that a personal God behave like an impersonal force — which is exactly the philosophical move the Gauḍīyas refuse.
    • Yoga-māyā sounds like a convenient narrative device — whenever the story needs a miracle, the spiritual potency shows up. Isn't this just pre-modern people explaining away coincidence?
      Notice what the purport actually claims: yoga-māyā is the Lord's spiritual potency, distinct from the māyā that bewilders even Brahmā. The point is not 'magic intervention' but that the Lord stays in spiritual touch with His devotees through a potency that is non-different from Him. You are free to remain skeptical of the Mahā-purāṇa's narrative, but the philosophical claim is testable in your own life: do you find that as you take to sādhana — chanting, hearing, serving — circumstances arrange themselves toward your spiritual progress in ways that exceed your planning? Pure devotees across centuries report exactly this. Yoga-māyā is the name for that organizing intelligence. The verse is not asking you to believe in a deus ex machina; it is asking you to begin practicing and watch what happens.

    The Lord ordered Yoga-māyā: O My potency, who are worshipable for the entire world and whose nature is to bestow good fortune upon all living entities, go to Vraja, where there live many cowherd men and their wives. In that very beautiful land, where many cows reside, Rohiṇī, the wife of Vasudeva, is living at the home of Nanda Mahārāja. Other wives of Vasudeva are also living there incognito because of fear of Kaṁsa. Please go there.
    Purport

    Nanda-gokula, the residence of King Nanda, was itself very beautiful, and when Yoga-māyā was ordered to go there and encourage the devotees with fearlessness, it became even more beautiful and safe. Because Yoga-māyā had the ability to create such an atmosphere, the Lord ordered her to go to Nanda-gokula.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Lord ordered Yogamāyā: O My potency, who are worshipable for the entire world and whose nature is to bestow good fortune upon all living entities, go to Vraja, where there live many cowherd men and their wives. In that very beautiful land, where many cows reside, Rohiṇī, the wife of Vasudeva, is living at the home of Nanda Mahārāja. Other wives of Vasudeva are also living there incognito because of fear of Kaṁsa. Please go there.
    Commentary

    After Devaki’s six children were killed, Vasudeva, seeing Rohini pregnant, sent her secretly to Gokula. Others also, being afraid of Kamsa (kamsa samvigna), lived in secret places (vivaresu—literally holes).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O Devī, worshipped by the world, full of all auspiciousness! He addresses her in this way to inspire her. Or the words show her qualification for going to Vraja. The other words also are meant to inspire her. The cowherds and cows are most astonishing, unimaginable by her. Other wives of Vasudeva were also living there.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself dispatches Yoga-māyā to Vraja so His devotees may live in fearless beauty — His protection precedes our awareness of it.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one place in your day where fear has quietly settled in, and consciously remember that Kṛṣṇa has already arranged shelter for those who take refuge in Him.
    • Speak to one devotee today as Vasudeva's wives lived in Nanda-gokula — incognito, sheltered, sustained by association rather than by external safety.
    • Refuse to treat the world's threats as the final word; before sleep tonight, name one 'Kaṁsa' in your life and entrust it to the Lord's potency rather than your own strategy.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I, like Vasudeva's other wives, hiding in 'caves' out of fear of some Kaṁsa — a person, an outcome, a worldly threat — instead of trusting Kṛṣṇa's arrangement to place me where I truly need to be?
    • If Yoga-māyā is the one who makes a place safe and beautiful for devotional service, what 'Nanda-gokula' am I being asked to relocate to today — what setting, association, or sādhana — that I keep postponing because I'd rather engineer my own security?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your friend group the way Krishna audited Vraja: who are the 'gopas and cows' — the unglamorous, steady people who make your life spiritually safe — and who are the Kaṁsa-figures whose presence keeps you living incognito, hiding the parts of you that actually want to chant, study, or behave well? This week, spend one more hour with the first group and one less with the second.
    • Notice where you are 'living in vivareṣu' — hiding your sādhana inside your own life out of fear of being mocked on the group chat or in the dorm. Pick one small practice (a tulasī mālā, a verse on your lock screen, declining a party for an ārati) that you stop hiding this week. Watch what fear surfaces; that fear is your Kaṁsa.
    • Before your next exam or big submission, do what Krishna did: send Yoga-māyā ahead. That means preparing the environment (clean desk, phone in another room, one round of japa) before you sit down — not relying on willpower in a hostile setting. Real vairāgya at your age is environmental, not heroic.
    householder
    • Treat your home as Nanda-gokula in miniature: ask whether it is currently 'gopa-gobhir alaṅkṛtam' — adorned by simple, devotional things (kitchen prasāda, a clean altar, regular guests who chant) — or adorned by screens, clutter, and ambient anxiety. Pick one room this month and re-decorate it according to the verse's standard, not the catalog's.
    • Identify the Kaṁsa in your family's life — the pressure (career ladder, school rankings, in-laws' expectations, mortgage fear) that has your spouse and children quietly 'living incognito,' hiding their devotional inclinations to keep peace. Have one direct conversation this week naming it, and decide together which fear you will stop organizing your household around.
    • Before launching the next big family decision (move, school change, job switch), explicitly invite Yoga-māyā first: a week of extra japa, consultation with a senior devotee, and an honest check on whether the move serves the soul or only the body. Do not confuse providing for your children's bodies with protecting their souls — the Gītā's whole pivot applies inside your own house.
    senior
    • Krishna chose to descend in a cowherd village, not a capital — and you are now in the season of life where you can actually choose the same. Begin loosening one attachment to status, property, or position this quarter, not as renunciation theater but as a real handover, so that what remains of your life is increasingly 'gopa-gobhir alaṅkṛtam' rather than résumé-shaped.
    • Become Yoga-māyā for someone younger: go ahead of them and prepare the ground. That means a phone call to a struggling grandchild, a letter to a former colleague, an introduction between two devotees who should know each other. At your stage, the most important work is no longer your own arrival but arranging the safe village others will arrive into.
    • Sit with the fact that Vasudeva's wives lived in Vraja in fear of Kaṁsa — and that Kaṁsa, in your life, is now mortality itself. Where are you still 'living incognito,' postponing the hard conversations, the unsaid forgiveness, the explicit instruction to your children about what to do with your body and your dharma when you go? Name one such postponement and address it this month, under Yoga-māyā's shelter, with dhairya rather than denial.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Yoga-māyā as a vague impersonal 'positive energy' or 'universe vibe,' rather than as Kṛṣṇa's personal potency acting under His direct order — collapsing the personalist line into generic spirituality.
    • Romanticizing Vraja as a faraway mythic landscape and missing the practical point: that the Lord himself arranges shelter and association for surrendered devotees here and now, in concrete circumstances.
    • Mistaking the wives' 'hiding incognito' for mere fearfulness and dismissing it, instead of recognizing strategic vairāgya — withdrawing from a Kaṁsa-dominated environment until Kṛṣṇa's arrangement matures — and so refusing to step back from toxic settings in one's own life when prudence calls for it.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Krishna sends Yoga-māyā ahead to prepare Nanda-gokula as a place of safety and beauty before the Lord's own descent. Where in your life have you tried to do Krishna's work without first letting His potency prepare the ground — and what broke as a result? Push back on each other if someone's answer sounds like spiritualized procrastination.
    • Vasudeva's other wives are living incognito in Vraja out of fear of Kaṁsa — yet that hiding is precisely what places them under Yoga-māyā's shelter. Is there a difference between cowardly hiding and protective concealment in spiritual life? Try to disagree before you agree.
    • The verse calls Vraja 'beautiful' specifically because of cowherds and cows, not because of palaces or wealth. If you had to name the equivalent 'gopa-gobhir alaṅkṛtam' of your own daily environment — the simple, unglamorous thing that actually makes a place spiritually safe — what would it be, and what does your answer reveal about what you currently value?
    Role Play

    A devotee couple has just received a job offer that would move them from a small Vaiṣṇava community (think: temple within walking distance, prasāda four nights a week, children running between four families' homes) to a much higher-paying role in a city where the nearest sādhu-saṅga is a two-hour drive. They sit down with a senior gṛhastha for advice. One person plays the husband (drawn to the salary, framing it as 'serving Krishna better with more resources'); one plays the wife (uneasy, citing this verse — that Krishna Himself chose Nanda-gokula for its cowherds and cows, not for opulence); one plays the senior devotee. After ten minutes, swap roles so the 'husband' must now defend the wife's position. The teacher then asks: where did each of you confuse material compassion (income, schools, safety) with real shelter under Yoga-māyā?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just mythology dressed up as instruction. Krishna 'sending' a goddess to 'prepare' a village reads like a fairy tale — what does it actually have to do with my life?
      Treat the verse as a description of how reality is arranged, not a bedtime story. Krishna acts through His potencies before He acts directly — the safe place exists before the Lord arrives in it. In your own life, notice that the conditions for serious sādhana are usually arranged for you long before you recognize them: the friend who first mentioned a verse, the illness that finally slowed you down, the disappointment that emptied a room in your heart. That is Yoga-māyā at work. You can either cooperate with that arrangement or insist on building your own Vraja out of ahaṅkāra and wonder why it never feels safe.
    • If Krishna is all-powerful, why does He need Yoga-māyā at all? Why the elaborate machinery — sending a potency, hiding wives, arranging incognito living — instead of just protecting devotees directly?
      The 'machinery' is the point, not a workaround. Krishna's relationships are personal, and personal relationships require distinct persons — a potency who acts, devotees who fear and are reassured, a Vraja that can be made beautiful. An impersonal Absolute would simply zap the problem; Krishna instead orchestrates a līlā in which Yoga-māyā, Rohiṇī, Nanda, and the cows each have a real role. This is the difference the Gauḍīya line insists on: surrender is not absorption into a featureless light, it is entering a living arrangement. Your sādhana, too, is meant to take place inside that arrangement — not in some private direct line that bypasses guru, devotees, and the protective veil His potency draws around the practitioner.

    Within the womb of Devakī is My partial plenary expansion known as Saṅkarṣaṇa or Śeṣa. Without difficulty, transfer Him into the womb of Rohiṇī.
    Purport

    The first plenary expansion of Kṛṣṇa is Baladeva, also known as Śeṣa. The Śeṣa incarnation of the Supreme Personality of Godhead supports the entire universe, and the eternal mother of this incarnation is mother Rohiṇī. “Because I am going into the womb of Devakī,” the Lord told Yoga-māyā, “the Śeṣa incarnation has already gone there and made suitable arrangements so that I may live there. Now He should enter the womb of Rohiṇī, His eternal mother.” In this connection, one may ask how the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is always situated transcendentally, could enter the womb of Devakī, which had previously been entered by the six asuras, the ṣaḍ-garbhas. Does this mean that the ṣaḍ-garbhāsuras were equal to the transcendental body of the Supreme Personality of Godhead? The following answer is given by Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura. The entire creation, as well as its individual parts, is an expansion of the energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore, even though the Lord enters the material world, He does not do so. This is explained by the Lord Himself in Bhagavad-gītā (9.4-5): mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad avyakta-mūrtinā mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ na ca mat-sthāni bhūtāni paśya me yogam aiśvaram bhūta-bhṛn na ca bhūta-stho mamātmā bhūta-bhāvanaḥ “By Me, in My unmanifested form, this entire universe is pervaded. All beings are in Me, but I am not in them. And yet everything that is created does not rest in Me. Behold My mystic opulence! Although I am the maintainer of all living entities, and although I am everywhere, My Self is the very source of creation.” Sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma. Everything is an expansion of Brahman, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, yet everything is not the Supreme Godhead, and He is not everywhere. Everything rests upon Him and yet does not rest upon Him. This can be explained only through the acintya-bhedābheda philosophy. Such truths cannot be understood, however, unless one is a pure devotee, for the Lord says in Bhagavad-gītā (18.55) , bhaktyā mām abhijānāti yāvān yaś cāsmi tattvataḥ: “One can understand the Supreme Personality as He is only by devotional service.” Even though the Lord cannot be understood by ordinary persons, this principle should be understood from the statement of the śāstras. A pure devotee is always transcendentally situated because of executing nine different processes of bhakti-yoga ( śravaṇaṁ kīrtanaṁ viṣṇoḥ smaranaṁ pāda-sevanam/ arcanaṁ vandanaṁ dāsyaṁ sakhyam ātma-nivedanam ). Thus situated in devotional service, a devotee, although in the material world, is not in the material world. Yet a devotee always fears, “Because I am associated with the material world, so many contaminations affect me.” Therefore he is always alert in fear, which gradually diminishes his material association. Symbolically, mother Devakī’s constant fear of Kaṁsa was purifying her. A pure devotee should always fear material association, and in this way all the asuras of material association will be killed, as the ṣaḍ-garbhāsuras were killed by Kaṁsa. It is said that from the mind, Marīci appears. In other words, Marīci is an incarnation of the mind. Marīci has six sons: Kāma, Krodha, Lobha, Moha, Mada and Mātsarya (lust, anger, greed, illusion, madness and envy). The Supreme Personality of Godhead appears in pure devotional service. This is confirmed in the Vedas: bhaktir evainaṁ darśayati. Only bhakti can bring one in contact with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The Supreme Personality of Godhead appeared from the womb of Devakī, and therefore Devakī symbolically represents bhakti, and Kaṁsa symbolically represents material fear. When a pure devotee always fears material association, his real position of bhakti is manifested, and he naturally becomes uninterested in material enjoyment. When the six sons of Marīci are killed by such fear and one is freed from material contamination, within the womb of bhakti the Supreme Personality of Godhead appears. Thus the seventh pregnancy of Devakī signifies the appearance of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. After the six sons Kāma, Krodha, Lobha, Moha, Mada and Mātsarya are killed, the Śeṣa incarnation creates a suitable situation for the appearance of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In other words, when one awakens his natural Kṛṣṇa consciousness, Lord Kṛṣṇa appears. This is the explanation given by Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Within the womb of Devakī is My partial plenary expansion known as Saṅkarṣaṇa or Śeṣa. Without difficulty, transfer Him into the womb of Rohiṇī.
    Commentary

    Mamakam dhama means that Baladeva is my amsa. Sesa is his portion. This is shown in verses such as sb 10.65.28; yasyaikamsensa vidhrta jagati jagatah pateh: O master of the universe, Rama! By one of your parts you hold up the earth." "Though Rohini is the eternal mother of Balarama, because of my request, he appeared in Devaki’s womb first. After establishing Sesa, his amsa there, as my bed and seat, He desired to go to the womb of his own mother." How is it possible that the first six material children could appear in the womb of Devaki, who is the pure spiritual energy of the pure Lord? Just as the material universes exist within the Supreme Lord but do not contaminate the Lord, so the six children could exist within Devaki without contaminating her. This is proven in the Gita: mat sthani sarva bhutani na caham tesv avastithah... The conjunction of material and spiritual in the pastimes is there to illustrate the methodical nature of bhakti. While devotees perform sadhana bhakti in the form of hearing and chanting internally there exists material enjoyment of the six objects of the senses (sound, touch, form, taste, smell and thought) as well, which is a secondary effect of bhakti. The devotee then cries out pitifully, "OH, because of this enjoyment I will fall into the material well of darkness. " By manifesting fear of material enjoyment, gradually the tendency to enjoy matter subsides. Then bhakti in the form of hearing and chanting the names, and glorifying the forms, qualities and pastimes of the Lord and serving in various ways, becomes prominent. Finally the Lord himself, the ocean of all wonderful forms and qualities appears within the devotee. Bhakti is suddha sattva by nature, and directly manifests the Lord. The sruti says: bhaktir evainam darsayati. Devotion makes the Lord reveal himself. As it is said that Marici appeared from the mind, he can be considered the incarnation of the mind. His six children are the six objects of the senses: sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and thought. As she possesses the power to make the Lord appear, Devaki can be considered the incarnation of bhakti. Kamsa can be considered the incarnation of fear, as it is often said "out of fear of Kamsa". Just as fear of the material world removes the six sense objects from the womb of bhakti, so Kamsa destroyed the six children of Devaki. Just as prema, characterized by intense service to the Lord, necessarily appears in the womb of bhakti after the desire for sense objects is extinguished, so Ananta, the form of service to the Lord, appeared as the seventh child of Devaki. Just as the Lord himself appears after prema bhakti appears, so Bhagavan himself appears as the eighth child of Devaki after Sesa appears.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Place the embryo (garbham), the form (dhāma) of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is my portion (mama), who is known as Śeṣa into Rohiṇī’s womb. Śeṣa means “he who remains.’ Dhāma can also mean the shelter, since he possesses the ādhāra-śakti, the power to maintain everything. Take the embryo invisibly and with joy (sam), by all means (ni).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Place the embryo (garbham), the form (dhāma) of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is my portion (mama), who is known as Śeṣa, into Rohiṇī’s womb. Śeṣa means “he who remains.’ Dhāma can also mean the shelter, since he possesses the ādhāra-śakti, the power to maintain everything. Take the embryo invisibly and with joy (sam), by all means (ni). “If he is called Śeṣa, why transfer him out of fear of Kaṁsa?” He is my shelter (dhāma māmakam). Or transfer him to Gokula (dhāma). Without him I cannot fulfill the happiness of my pastimes there.

    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Devakī's constant fear of Kaṁsa is bhakti's purifying alertness — when the six inner asuras (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya) are slain, Kṛṣṇa appears within.
    Practical Applications
    • Name today which of the six — kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, or mātsarya — is most active in you, and refuse it one specific indulgence before sundown.
    • Cultivate Devakī's sat-bhaya: each time material association tempts you (a scroll, a grudge, a craving), pause and say aloud, 'This contaminates the womb where Kṛṣṇa would appear.'
    • Begin the day with one of the nine processes of bhakti — śravaṇaṁ or kīrtanaṁ — for ten unbroken minutes, treating it as Śeṣa preparing the ground for the Lord's arrival in your consciousness.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which 'asuras' — kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya — is still gestating in the womb of my consciousness, and what specific material association keeps feeding it?
    • Where in my life am I mistaking comfortable association with the material world for safety, when in fact it is the very fearlessness Devakī did not have that is blocking Kṛṣṇa's appearance in me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your phone today the way Devakī watched Kaṁsa: which apps and group chats are the six asuras (lust, anger, greed, illusion, madness, envy) sneaking in through? Don't delete anything dramatically — just notice, with the same alert fear Devakī had, what is entering the womb of your attention.
    • Before your next exam or interview, instead of pumping yourself up with 'I've got this,' try the opposite: acknowledge that the outcome is being arranged by a higher energy (Yoga-māyā), and your job is only to show up cleanly prepared. Notice whether this lowers or raises your performance.
    • Identify one friendship where you are the Rohiṇī — the safer, steadier womb — for someone who is in a Devakī-like situation (toxic family, hostile dorm, controlling relationship). Without preaching, be that protected space for them this week.
    householder
    • Treat your home as the womb in which Kṛṣṇa-consciousness is gestating for your children. This week, name out loud one specific 'Kaṁsa' you are choosing to keep out — a show, a habit of speech, a category of conversation — and one 'Rohiṇī-arrangement' you are putting in place (a kīrtana time, a meal together, a verse on the fridge).
    • In your next significant family or career decision, explicitly ask: am I trying to be Yoga-māyā here — orchestrating outcomes — or am I willing to be Rohiṇī, the receptive arrangement Kṛṣṇa transfers things into? Discuss with your spouse where the line is.
    • Pick the one of the six sons of Marīci (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya) that most disturbs your household — usually krodha or lobha for working parents — and for one week treat its arising as a fire alarm for sādhana, not a personal failing. Each time it arises, chant one round.
    senior
    • You have already 'transferred wombs' many times — childhood body to youth to middle age to now. Sit with that lineage of transitions today and feel that the same Self has been carried through each one without difficulty by Yoga-māyā. Let this rehearse you for the final transfer.
    • Identify a younger devotee or family member who is in a hostile environment for their spiritual life. Become consciously their Rohiṇī this season: the safe womb they can transfer their tender bhakti into. Mentor without controlling.
    • Of the six asuras, mada (pride in past accomplishments) and mātsarya (envy of those still in their prime) tend to grip seniors most. Name the one that is yours, and treat its arising not as shameful but as the very contamination Devakī's fear was meant to burn off — let it sharpen your chanting rather than depress you.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the transfer of Śeṣa as mere mythological mechanics and missing the inner instruction — that the Lord's appearance in the heart requires a prior arranging by His expansion through purificatory fear of material contamination.
    • Cultivating a vague 'spiritual fear' as a mood, while still nurturing the six sons of Marīci in daily habits — being afraid in theory of māyā but unafraid in practice of lust, anger, greed, illusion, madness, and envy.
    • Concluding from 'everything is Brahman' that the Lord's descent into Devakī's womb proves He is materially contaminated like the ṣaḍ-garbhāsuras — collapsing acintya-bhedābheda into flat impersonalism and losing the personal Kṛṣṇa to whom surrender is owed.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī's constant fear of Kaṁsa is presented as purifying, not as a defect. Share with your partner: where in your life is fear functioning as a purifying alarm bell, and where is it just neurosis? How do you tell the difference without rationalizing one as the other?
    • Prabhupāda names the six sons of Marīci — kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya — as the asuras Kaṁsa kills. Pick the one that has the strongest grip on you right now, and disagree with each other honestly: is fearing material association actually a workable strategy against it, or does avoidance just feed the very thing you're trying to escape?
    • The verse says Śeṣa is transferred from Devakī's womb to Rohiṇī's 'without difficulty' by Yoga-māyā. In your own sādhana, what have you been trying to muscle through with willpower that the verse suggests is actually arranged by Kṛṣṇa's energy? Where does the line fall between your effort and His arrangement — and do you and your partner draw that line in the same place?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a sincere devotee who has just received a job offer in a new city — better pay, but it would mean leaving an established sanga and moving into an environment full of material association (corporate culture, colleagues uninterested in spiritual life, evening entertainment). Student A is genuinely afraid of the contamination but also worries this fear is just cowardice or attachment to comfort. Student B is a senior devotee Student A trusts. Student B must respond using the verse's logic — that fear of material association can itself be purifying like Devakī's, that the six asuras (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya) need to be confronted not just avoided, and that Kṛṣṇa arranges the womb in which He will appear. Do not give a yes/no answer. Help Student A discern which fear is bhakti-fear and which is bodily fear. Swap roles after eight minutes.

    Objections & Responses
    • Teaching people to 'always fear material association' sounds psychologically harmful. Modern wellness teaches us that anxiety is the disease, not the cure. Won't this verse just produce scrupulous, paranoid devotees?
      The fear Prabhupāda describes is not anxiety in the clinical sense — it is sajātīya-bhaya, the wakefulness of someone who knows what is at stake. A new mother does not have an anxiety disorder because she is alert to what could harm her infant; she is simply awake to the value of what she is carrying. Devakī carried Kṛṣṇa Himself, and her fear of Kaṁsa was the natural alertness of one who knows the worth of what is within. The Gauḍīya line distinguishes this carefully from rajasic worry about outcomes or tamasic dread. Bhakti-fear does not paralyze; it sharpens. Notice that Devakī continues her duties throughout. The test is fruit: does your 'spiritual fear' make you more present, more careful with the holy name, more honest about your associations — or does it spiral inward? If the latter, that is not what this verse describes.
    • The whole transfer-of-the-embryo story is biologically absurd. Treating it as literal makes the tradition look credulous; treating it as allegory means we should just teach the moral and drop the narrative.
      The verse does not ask you to choose between literal history and inner meaning — Vyāsadeva, through Śukadeva, gives both at once, and Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura's commentary that Prabhupāda relays here shows precisely how. Yoga-māyā, Kṛṣṇa's internal potency, performs the transfer; this is not biology, it is acintya-śakti, the inconceivable energy by which the Lord enters the material world without being touched by it (Gītā 9.4–5, quoted right in the purport). To 'drop the narrative' is to lose the very thing the allegory is anchored in — that Kṛṣṇa is a person who acts, who sends Yoga-māyā, who arranges the appearance of His own brother. Impersonalists will always want the moral without the Lord. The Gauḍīya answer is that the pastime and the inner meaning are non-different — acintya-bhedābheda — and the strength of one depends on holding the other.
