    O all-auspicious Yoga-māyā, I shall then appear with My full six opulences as the son of Devakī, and you will appear as the daughter of mother Yaśodā, the queen of Mahārāja Nanda.
    Purport

    The word aṁśa-bhāgena is important in this verse. In Bhagavad-gītā (10.42) the Lord says: athavā bahunaitena kiṁ jñātena tavārjuna viṣṭabhyāham idaṁ kṛtsnam ekāṁśena sthito jagat “But what need is there, Arjuna, for all this detailed knowledge? With a single fragment of Myself I pervade and support this entire universe.” Everything is situated as a part of the Supreme Lord’s potency. In regard to Lord Kṛṣṇa’s appearance in the womb of Devakī, Brahmā played a part also because on the bank of the Milk Ocean he requested the Supreme Personality of Godhead to appear. A part was also played by Baladeva, the first expansion of Godhead. Similarly, Yoga-māyā, who appeared as the daughter of mother Yaśodā, also played a part. Thus jīva-tattva, viṣṇu-tattva and śakti-tattva are all integrated with the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and when Kṛṣṇa appears, He appears with all His integrated parts. As explained in previous verses, Yoga-māyā was requested to attract Saṅkarṣaṇa, Baladeva, from the womb of Devakī to the womb of Rohiṇī, and this was a very heavy task for her. Yoga-māyā naturally could not see how it was possible for her to attract Saṅkarṣaṇa. Therefore Kṛṣṇa addressed her as śubhe, auspicious, and said, “Be blessed. Take power from Me, and you will be able to do it.” By the grace of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, anyone can do anything, for the Lord is present in everything, all things being His parts and parcels ( aṁśa-bhāgena ) and increasing or decreasing by His supreme will. Balarāma was only fifteen days older than Kṛṣṇa. By the blessings of Kṛṣṇa, Yoga-māyā became the daughter of mother Yaśodā, but by the supreme will she was not able to enjoy the parental love of her father and mother. Kṛṣṇa, however, although not actually born from the womb of mother Yaśodā, enjoyed the parental love of mother Yaśodā and Nanda. By the blessings of Kṛṣṇa, Yoga-māyā was able to achieve the reputation of being the daughter of mother Yaśodā, who also became famous by the blessings of Kṛṣṇa. Yaśodā means “one who gives fame.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O all-auspicious Yogamāyā, I shall then appear with My full six opulences as the son of Devakī, and you will appear as the daughter of mother Yaśodā, the queen of Mahārāja Nanda.
    Commentary

    Amsa bhaga means that knowledge, strength and other secondary qualities (amsa) accompany (bhaga=bhajana) the Lord so that he manifests completely. "I will appear as the son of Devaki with all qualities." This is Sridhara Swami’s explanation of the words in Bhavartha Dipika. According to Jiva Goswami in Vaisnava tosani there are two meanings. He is perfect in whom all the parts (amsa) enter (bhajana= pravesa or entrance). "I will appear as Devaki’s son perfect with all parts." Another meaning of the words is that amsa refers to Brahma and all other servants and bhaga refers to auspiciousness. The Lord appears for the auspiciousness of Brahma and others. " I will appear as the son of Devaki for the welfare of Brahma and others." Or another meaning is as follows. Bhaga means amsa "I will appear in the mood of a son of Devaki as a part of a part, or partially manifesting myself, not completely. Devaki will love me only with aisvarya bhava. Yasoda will manifest complete parental love for me, devoid of the restriction of aisvarya. But you, Yogamaya will simply appear from Yasoda (bhavisyasi)." It is not mentioned that she will become the daughter of Yasoda, though it is mentioned that Krsna will become the son (putratam) of Devaki. "She will not have affection for you as her daughter. Your presence in Vraja will not be noticed by anyone."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Then, very soon after, the Lord says he will appear as the son of Devakī. Later it will be explained that Baladeva was only slightly older in birth. Śrīdhara Svāmī explained the word aṁśa as follows. Bhāgena may be formed from bhaj, to possess. Thus the meaning is “existing with all his śaktis.” Or it can mean “endowed with all his qualities like knowledge and power.” Or it can mean “with the form who glances at māyā as the puruṣa.” Or it can mean “with a form which enters into all his expansions.” Or it can mean “with a form bestowing auspiciousness to jīvas like Brahmā.” Dūrgā may ask, “What is my qualification for being born to Yaśodā?” Kṛṣṇa says “O auspicious one (śubhe)!” By my order, you attain auspiciousness and thus have attained qualification. This is a benediction. This means she will be able to bewilder Nanda and others. Of the word suggests “Because you will appear in Yaśodā you will have fame (yaśaḥ) and bliss (nanda).” The confidential meaning is this. With different (bhāgena) forms (aṁśa) I will appear as the son of Devakī and also as the son of Yaśodā. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains that the word svāṁśena in the verse avatīrṇau jagaty-arthe svāṁśena bala-keśavau (SB 10.38.32) to mean “with their distinct forms.” And you will be present in Yaśodā (bhaviṣyati) but not has her daughter. This meaning can be understood because of the use of different verbs (prāpysāmi and bhaviṣyati). And if the same verb were used for both statements then it would be understood that Durgā would be born as the son of Yaśodā. But calling a girl a son must be rejected by resorting to normal usage as śruti statements like pumāṁsām putram ādhehi: place a son with Viṣṇu’ṣ form in the womb. Just as Devakī carried the Lord in her heart (SB 10.2.18) so Yaśodā also carried the Lord. Just as I take Devakī as a mother, I also take Yaśodā as my mother. Śukadeva will describe this later “Kṛṣṇa appeared as Nanda’s son.” (SB 10.5.1) Thus you will just make a show of your potency since you are māyā.

    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa descends with His full six opulences as Devakī's son, while Yoga-māyā appears as Yaśodā's daughter — every part of His pastime is empowered by Him alone.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you assume credit for outcomes — quietly remember that whatever capacity you have is aṁśa-bhāgena, a fragment of His potency loaned to you.
    • When asked to do something heavier than you feel able to bear, pray as Yoga-māyā did and proceed, trusting His śubhe blessing rather than your own measured strength.
    • Refuse the impersonalist habit of crediting 'the universe' — speak Kṛṣṇa's name explicitly when offering one task back to Him this evening.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I trying to act as the sole 'doer' — when in truth, like Yoga-māyā needing Kṛṣṇa's śubhe blessing to attract Saṅkarṣaṇa, I am only a part being moved by His potency?
    • What 'heavy task' is currently before me that feels impossible by my own strength, and how would my approach change today if I treated it as something I can only accomplish aṁśa-bhāgena — by taking power from Him rather than from myself?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick one group project, club role, or study-group task this week where you have been quietly coasting because 'someone else will carry it' — own your aṁśa, your part, fully, even if it is small and unseen.
    • Yoga-māyā told Kṛṣṇa the task looked impossible; He said śubhe, take power from Me. Before your next exam or hard conversation, spend two minutes asking Kṛṣṇa for the strength specifically — not for the outcome — and notice how that changes your preparation.
    • Yaśodā got the love Devakī gave birth to. On social media you will constantly see peers receiving recognition you feel you earned. Today, when that sting hits, name it out loud as Devakī-feeling and refuse to post the subtle comparison — practice early vairāgya from the metric.
    householder
    • In one family or work decision this week, deliberately act as aṁśa-bhāgena — a contributing part, not the controlling whole. Make the decision, then explicitly hand the result to Kṛṣṇa instead of micromanaging the outcome with your spouse, child, or team.
    • Identify a 'heavy task' in your household or career you have been calling impossible — a hard conversation with a teenager, a financial restructuring, a career pivot. Say to Kṛṣṇa what Yoga-māyā heard: 'I cannot see how,' and ask for the śubhe-blessing. Then take the next concrete step today, not after more planning.
    • Yoga-māyā became the daughter of Yaśodā but could not enjoy parental love as a daughter. Notice today the roles in your household where you do the work without receiving the warmth — cooking unthanked, earning unappreciated, parenting unseen — and offer that specific unreciprocated portion to Kṛṣṇa as your real vairāgya, not a vacation from family life.
    senior
    • Yaśodā means 'one who gives fame,' and her fame came by Kṛṣṇa's blessing, not her biology. Pick one younger person — a grandchild, a junior colleague, a new devotee — and this month deliberately give them the fame: credit them publicly for something you could have claimed. Practice being the source, not the recipient, of yaśas.
    • Reflect that Kṛṣṇa Himself appears aṁśa-bhāgena, integrated with His parts. Make a written list of the 'parts' of your life-work — children, students, projects, possessions — and consciously demote each from 'mine' to 'a part He arranged.' Read the list at your evening sandhyā for one week and notice which item your heart refuses to release.
    • Balarāma was only fifteen days older than Kṛṣṇa, yet stepped aside from Devakī's womb so the līlā could unfold. As a senior, identify one role — in the temple, family, or community — where your continued presence is more habit than service, and take the Balarāma-step: arrange your own transfer to Rohiṇī while you still can, training a successor before mortality forces the transition.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading aṁśa-bhāgena as if Kṛṣṇa Himself is only a part or fragment of some larger Absolute — inverting the verse, which actually says the entire cosmos is sustained by a single fragment of Him; this slides into impersonalism and demotes Kṛṣṇa from supreme Personality of Godhead to one expression among many.
    • Using 'everything is His potency' as a quietist excuse to abdicate responsibility — sitting back and saying 'Kṛṣṇa will do it through me' without actually doing the heavy task in front of you; Yoga-māyā still had to act, she simply acted on borrowed power.
    • Romanticizing Yaśodā's parental love while overlooking the verse's harder teaching — that Yoga-māyā, by supreme will, was denied the parental affection her 'sister' Kṛṣṇa enjoyed; mistaking devotional service for a guarantee of the sweet outcomes we want, rather than a placement assigned by His will.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kṛṣṇa says He will appear with His full six opulences (aṁśa-bhāgena) while Yoga-māyā plays an integrated 'part.' Where in your own service do you confuse playing your part with claiming the whole credit — and where do you refuse a part because it isn't the whole? Disagree with each other honestly.
    • Yoga-māyā 'naturally could not see how it was possible' to do what Kṛṣṇa asked, and Kṛṣṇa answered 'śubhe — take power from Me.' Share a current task you have privately written off as impossible. Push back on each other: is this real impossibility, or refusal disguised as humility?
    • Yaśodā received the parental love that Devakī biologically earned; Yoga-māyā took the form of a daughter she could not enjoy as a daughter. Where in your own life have you been given Devakī's role and where Yaśodā's — and which one secretly stings? Do not let each other off with pious answers.
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a senior devotee asked by the temple president to step down from a visible preaching role and instead train a younger devotee behind the scenes — 'aṁśa-bhāgena, just a part.' Student B is the younger devotee being elevated, who privately suspects A is being shelved unfairly and feels guilty taking the spot. Play out a fifteen-minute conversation where A must speak from the position of Yoga-māyā being told 'take power from Me and do this heavy task,' and B must respond as someone receiving Yaśodā's unearned good fortune. The teacher pauses the scene at any point either student slips into vague spirituality or false humility, and asks: 'What would real vairāgya sound like here, right now?'

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole verse is mythological stage-management — Kṛṣṇa assigning roles to Yoga-māyā, choosing wombs, arranging swaps. It reads like a script, not a revelation. Why should a modern reader take it as anything more than ancient narrative theater?
      The 'stage-management' is precisely the point: the verse insists that nothing in Kṛṣṇa's appearance is accidental, including the apparently small parts. Modern readers are trained to dismiss what feels arranged because we worship spontaneity. But the Bhāgavatam is showing the opposite — that jīva-tattva, viṣṇu-tattva and śakti-tattva all cooperate by the Lord's will, and that even Brahmā on the bank of the Milk Ocean played a part. If you take it as theater, you reduce yourself to an audience. If you take it as the structure of reality, you become a participant who can also be assigned a part — and that is what sādhana is. The choice the verse forces is not believe-or-disbelieve; it is spectator-or-servant.
    • Telling Yoga-māyā 'take power from Me' and then telling us the same is just a religious version of 'manifest your dreams.' It is empowerment language dressed in Sanskrit. Where is the actual difference?
      The difference is the direction of dependence. 'Manifest your dreams' locates the power in you and makes Kṛṣṇa, if mentioned at all, an accessory to your agenda. Kṛṣṇa's word to Yoga-māyā is the inverse: the task is His, the power is His, and she is asked to surrender her own assessment ('I cannot see how this is possible') and become an instrument. Notice that Yoga-māyā does not get to enjoy being Yaśodā's daughter — empowerment without personal payoff is not what self-help sells. This is bhakti: you accept a heavy assignment, you draw strength from Him, and you do not collect the fruit. Test it by the fruits clause — anything that ends in your enlargement is the modern myth; anything that ends in His service is the verse.

    By sacrifices of animals, ordinary human beings will worship you gorgeously, with various paraphernalia, because you are supreme in fulfilling the material desires of everyone.
    Purport

    As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (7.20) , kāmais tais tair hṛta jñānāḥ prapadyante ’nya-devatāḥ: “Those whose minds are distorted by material desires surrender unto demigods.” Therefore the word manuṣya, meaning “human being,” here refers to one who does not know the actual goal of life. Such a person wants to enjoy the material world by taking birth in a highly elevated family with the benefits of education, beauty and immense wealth, which in this material world are desirable. One who has forgotten the real aim of life may worship the goddess Durgā, māyā-śakti, under various names, for different purposes, and in different places. As there are many holy places for the worship of Kṛṣṇa, there are also many holy places in India for the worship of Durgādevī, or Māyādevī, who took birth as the daughter of Yaśodā. After cheating Kaṁsa, Māyādevī dispersed herself to various places, especially in Vindhyācala, to accept regular worship from ordinary men. A human being should actually be interested in understanding ātma-tattva, the truth of ātmā, the spirit soul, and Paramātmā, the supreme soul. Those who are interested in ātma-tattva worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead ( yasmin vijñāte sarvam evaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati ) ( Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.3). However, as explained in the next verse of this chapter, those who cannot understand ātma-tattva ( apaśyatām ātma-tattvam ) worship Yoga-māyā in her different features. Therefore Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (2.1.2) says: śrotavyādīni rājendra nṛṇāṁ santi sahasraśaḥ apaśyatām ātma-tattvaṁ gṛheṣu gṛha-medhinām “Those persons who are materially engrossed, being blind to the knowledge of ultimate truth, have many subject matters for hearing in human society, O Emperor.” Those who are interested in remaining in this material world and are not interested in spiritual salvation have many duties, but for one who is interested in spiritual salvation, the only duty is to surrender fully unto Kṛṣṇa ( sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja ). Such a person is not interested in material enjoyment.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    By sacrifices of animals, ordinary human beings will worship you gorgeously, with various paraphernalia, because you are supreme in fulfilling the material desires of everyone.
    Commentary

    Your amsa, maha maya, will be taken by Vasudeva to cheat Kamsa. You will be worshipped in various forms in Vindhacala and other places. All men will worship these forms, because you are the supreme (varam) goddess (isvarim) of those who have all types of material desires.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Three verses elaborate. Because men have desires and are qualified with that dharma, you bestow benedictions. Hari-vaṁśa says pradāṁ te kariṣyāmi mat prabhāva-amaṁ bhuvi Yena sarvasya lokasya devi devī bhavisyasi O Devī! I give you power equal to mine in this world by which you will become the goddess of all men.

    Related values & verses
    Related values

    Related verses
    SB 10.2.7 SB 10.2.8 SB 10.2.9 SB 10.2.11 SB 10.2.13 BG 15.1 BG 9.11 BG 15.2 BG 6.1 BG 6.47 BG 5.4 YS 2.45
    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Worship aimed at material desires keeps you a 'manuṣya' chasing fruits; the soul's only real duty is surrender to Kṛṣṇa.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice every prayer or wish you offered today and ask whether it sought a material fruit or Kṛṣṇa Himself, and re-aim it.
    • Refuse to treat Kṛṣṇa as one more demigod for boons — speak to Him today only as the goal, not the means.
    • Spend ten minutes studying ātma-tattva (read one purport on the soul) instead of consuming one round of entertainment.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which 'sarva-kāma' — which bundle of material desires — am I quietly hoping the spiritual path will fulfill, rather than dissolve?
    • Where in my worship or sādhana am I behaving like the manuṣya of this verse — approaching the Divine with elaborate offerings but a transactional heart, asking for fruits instead of seeking ātma-tattva?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your last ten prayers, wishes, or 'manifestations' — the ones whispered before exams, before opening grades, before checking who replied to your message. How many were requests to a sarva-kāma-vara-pradām figure (the universe, luck, a deity, your own willpower) for a material outcome? Write them down; the list itself is the lesson.
    • Pick one upcoming ambition — a grade, a placement, an admission, a relationship — and practice asking for the strength to do your duty (kartavya) toward it rather than for the result. Notice how much harder this prayer is, and how much it exposes about what you actually trust.
    • On social media this week, watch how often spiritual or aesthetic imagery (temples, deities, 'good vibes') is deployed to chase material kāma — followers, validation, aesthetic identity. Resolve not to post one such image yourself for seven days, and observe what withdrawal feels like. That withdrawal is your own manuṣya-mind meeting the verse.
    householder
    • Look honestly at the last big family decision — a school for a child, a house, a job change, a financial move. Was it a gṛhastha decision (household life ordered toward Kṛṣṇa) or a gṛha-medhī decision (household life as the end in itself)? Name the difference out loud to your spouse this week; do not solve it yet, just name it.
    • In your worship at home, separate two registers and keep them separate for a month: prayers of petition for the family's material needs (health, school, income) and prayers of offering with no agenda. Place the second one first — before the dīpa is lit, before the children are called — even if it is only two minutes.
    • Practice dāna and aparigraha together as a couple: choose one possession or one recurring expense this month that exists purely to fulfill kāma, and give the equivalent away. Tell your children why, in plain language. You are teaching them, by demonstration, that the household is not the highest court of appeal.
    senior
    • List the material boons you spent decades pursuing — career, status, the children's success, the house, the savings. Mark each one: did getting it free you, or did it generate the next desire? Sit with the pattern. This is the verse showing you your own life from the inside.
    • When you mentor a younger person this season, resist the temptation to bless them only with sarva-kāma-vara — 'may you get the job, the match, the promotion.' Bless them once, in your own words, with ātma-tattva: with the wish that they come to know the soul and the Supreme Soul. Watch how unfamiliar that blessing feels in your own mouth.
    • Choose one attachment — a possession, a role, an identity ('the one who provides,' 'the matriarch,' 'the expert') — and begin its formal handover this month. Not renunciation as performance; quiet, practical loosening. Use the time recovered for hearing and chanting. The body's transitions are coming; let the grip soften before they are pried open.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as a dismissal of Durgādevī or other devatās rather than as a precise diagnosis of the worshipper's motive — the pitfall is contempt for others' worship instead of scrutiny of one's own desires.
    • Assuming that because one worships Kṛṣṇa (and not a demigod), one is automatically free of the manuṣya-mentality — yet still approaching Kṛṣṇa with the same shopping-list of sarva-kāma, just addressed to a different name.
    • Mistaking the verse's critique of kāmya worship as a license to abandon ritual, offering, and arcana altogether, when the real correction is to retain the offerings (dhūpa, upahāra, bali of one's labor) but reorient them from material desire toward ātma-tattva and surrender.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda calls the worshippers in this verse manuṣya — 'human beings' — but redefines the word to mean those who have forgotten the actual goal of life. Where in your own week are you a 'manuṣya' in that diminished sense, approaching the sacred with a shopping list of material wants? Be specific with your partner; do not let each other off with generalities.
    • The verse names Māyādevī as sarva-kāma-vara-pradām — she really does grant material desires. So worshipping her 'works.' Discuss with your group: if it works, what exactly is wrong with it? Push back on each other until you can articulate the difference between getting what you asked for and getting what you actually need.
    • Prabhupāda contrasts the gṛha-medhī (one absorbed in household affairs as an end in themselves) with one who seeks ātma-tattva. Yet the householder āśrama is honored in our tradition. Where is the line between a legitimate gṛhastha life and the gṛha-medhī drift? Share one decision from the past month where you can feel the line in your own life.
    Role Play

    Two students are paired. Student A plays a sincere friend who has just returned from a Durgā-pūjā at a famous temple, glowing about the atmosphere and convinced she received a job offer because of the goddess's grace. She asks Student B — known in the friend group as 'the Krishna person' — whether she should keep going every year. Student B must respond as a Gauḍīya practitioner: honoring Māyādevī's actual position (the verse says she does grant such boons; she is Kṛṣṇa's internal energy who took birth as Yaśodā's daughter), not insulting the friend's experience, but gently turning the conversation toward ātma-tattva and the Personality of Godhead behind the energy. The teacher should stop the scene if Student B becomes either dismissive ('that's just demigod worship') or impersonalist ('it's all the same divine'). Run it twice, swapping roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse and purport sound condescending — it labels millions of sincere Durgā devotees as people who 'do not know the actual goal of life.' Isn't that exactly the kind of religious arrogance the modern world is right to reject?
      Notice that Prabhupāda is not insulting Māyādevī — he is honoring her as Kṛṣṇa's energy, the daughter of Yaśodā, worshipped at genuine holy places like Vindhyācala. The discrimination is not between 'our god' and 'their god'; it is between asking for the gift and asking for the Giver. A child who only ever asks his mother for sweets is not wicked, but he has not yet understood his mother. The Gītā verse Prabhupāda cites — kāmais tais tair hṛta-jñānāḥ — is diagnostic, not contemptuous. We say the same thing about ourselves whenever we approach Kṛṣṇa with a material agenda. The verse is a mirror first, a critique second.
    • If Māyādevī genuinely fulfills material desires, and material life is what most people actually want, then this whole framework is just spiritual elitism dressed up as compassion. Why shouldn't ordinary people get the births, beauty, and wealth they're asking for?
      They should — and the verse confirms they do. Nothing in the purport denies that the boons come. The question is not whether the system works but where it ends. Take birth, beauty, education, wealth: walk each one to its terminus. Each ends in old age, disease, and another body, with the desires intact and the bill compounding. Prabhupāda's compassion is precisely not to interrupt anyone's pūjā but to whisper: there is one more thing you can ask for that does not have to be asked for again. That is ātma-tattva, and finally surrender to Kṛṣṇa Himself — sarva-dharmān parityajya. To withhold that whisper out of politeness would be the real elitism: deciding in advance that other people cannot bear the higher offer.

    Lord Kṛṣṇa blessed Māyādevī by saying: In different places on the surface of the earth, people will give you different names, such as Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, Vaiṣṇavī, Kumudā, Caṇḍikā, Kṛṣṇā, Mādhavī, Kanyakā, Māyā, Nārāyaṇī, Īśānī, Śāradā and Ambikā.
    Purport

    Because Kṛṣṇa and His energy appeared simultaneously, people have generally formed two groups — the śāktas and the Vaiṣṇavas — and sometimes there is rivalry between them. Essentially, those who are interested in material enjoyment are śāktas, and those interested in spiritual salvation and attaining the spiritual kingdom are Vaiṣṇavas. Because people are generally interested in material enjoyment, they are interested in worshiping Māyādevī, the energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Vaiṣṇavas, however, are śuddha-śāktas, or pure bhaktas, because the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra indicates worship of the Supreme Lord’s energy, Harā. A Vaiṣṇava prays to the energy of the Lord for the opportunity to serve the Lord along with His spiritual energy. Thus Vaiṣṇavas all worship such Deities as Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, Sītā-Rāma, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Rukmiṇī-Dvārakādhīśa, whereas durgā-śāktas worship the material energy under different names. The names by which Māyādevī is known in different places have been listed by Vallabhācārya as follows. In Vārāṇasī she is known as Durgā, in Avantī she is known as Bhadrakālī, in Orissa she is known as Vijayā, and in Kulahāpura she is known as Vaiṣṇavī or Mahālakṣmī. (The representatives of Mahālakṣmī and Ambikā are present in Bombay.) In the country known as Kāmarūpa she is known as Caṇḍikā, in Northern India as Śāradā, and in Cape Comorin as Kanyakā. Thus she is distributed according to various names in various places. Śrīla Vijayadhvaja Tīrthapāda, in his Pada-ratnāvalī-ṭīkā, has explained the meanings of the different representations. Māyā is known as Durgā because she is approached with great difficulty, as Bhadrā because she is auspicious, and as Kālī because she is deep blue. Because she is the most powerful energy, she is known as Vijayā; because she is one of the different energies of Viṣṇu, she is known as Vaiṣṇavī; and because she enjoys in this material world and gives facilities for material enjoyment, she is known as Kumudā. Because she is very severe to her enemies, the asuras, she is known as Caṇḍikā, and because she gives all sorts of material facilities, she is called Kṛṣṇā. In this way the material energy is differently named and situated in different places on the surface of the globe.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Lord Kṛṣṇa blessed Māyādevī by saying: In different places on the surface of the earth, people will give you different names, such as Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, Vaiṣṇavī, Kumudā, Caṇḍikā, Kṛṣṇā, Mādhavī, Kanyakā, Māyā, Nārāyaṇī, Īśānī, Śāradā and Ambikā.
    Commentary

    Kurvanti (present tense) here indicates the future. "Men will call you by various names and establish many temples for you." This means "By my and your appearance on earth some men will become vaisnavas and others will become saktas."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The two verses are taken together. The future tense is meant. Men, situated on the earth, meaning all men, will make temples and give you different names. According to their particular desires with different attitudes towards your deity forms, they will give you names like Durgā. According to different places you will be known by different names. In some places you will be known by one name, in other places by two names and in other places by many names. The word ca indicates that these are the main names among all the names.

    SB 4.29.1 SB 10.2.8 SB 10.2.9 SB 10.2.10 SB 10.2.13 SB 10.2.14 BG 3.9 BG 4.24 BG 3.10 BG 8.4
    Concepts
    JivaMantraMaya
    Personal Guidance
    Māyādevī wears many names across the earth, but she remains Kṛṣṇa's energy — a Vaiṣṇava worships her only as Harā, the Lord's servant.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today when you are tempted to petition material energy under any of her names for enjoyment, and redirect that prayer to Kṛṣṇa through the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra.
    • Refuse the śākta-impulse to chase facilities for bodily enjoyment, and instead ask Harā for one concrete opportunity to serve Kṛṣṇa today.
    • Speak respectfully of Durgā, Kālī, and Caṇḍikā as Kṛṣṇa's energy — never as independent supreme deities — when the topic comes up with family or friends.
    Reflection Questions
    • Under which of Māyādevī's many names — security, beauty, prestige, family safety, intellectual mastery — am I most comfortably worshiping the material energy while telling myself I am being spiritual?
    • What would it actually look like, this week, for me to approach Harā as the Lord's spiritual energy and ask for service, rather than approaching her as Durgā and asking for material protection and provision?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit one week of your prayers — including the silent ones before exams, before posting, before texting a crush. How many were 'Kṛṣṇa, give me this result' (śākta) versus 'Kṛṣṇa, let me serve You through this' (Vaiṣṇava)? Write the count down; don't moralize, just see.
    • Pick one upcoming situation where you are tempted to ask the universe for a specific outcome — an admission, a follower count, a relationship. Practice nishkama-karma: do the work fully, and consciously decline to bargain with the energy for the fruit.
    • When friends say 'all gods are the same, pick whichever vibe you like,' resist both reactions — neither nodding along nor lecturing. Instead ask them, and yourself, 'same for what purpose? enjoyment or surrender?' Let that one question do the work.
    householder
    • Notice the family rituals where you are quietly approaching the Lord's energy for material results — a son's job, a daughter's match, a promotion, a court case. Keep doing them with full sincerity, but add one line at the end: 'and above all, let this household become Yours.' Re-aim the same act.
    • When making a household financial or career decision this month, apply discriminative wisdom: ask not only 'will this give us more comfort?' but 'will this give us more capacity to serve?' If the answer to the second is no, it is a śākta decision wearing a Vaiṣṇava costume — be honest about it.
    • Teach your children the names in this verse without flattening them. Tell them Durgā, Kālī, Caṇḍikā are real, powerful, and serve Kṛṣṇa — not rival gods, not the same as Kṛṣṇa. Children can hold this distinction earlier than we credit them; muddled parents produce muddled bhakti.
    senior
    • Look back at the last forty years of your prayers and vows. How much was addressed, in effect, to Māyādevī under one of her many names — for protection, prosperity, progeny, removal of obstacles? No regret; just clarity. Then redirect what remains of your prayer-life toward Kṛṣṇa Himself.
    • Practice tyāga concretely with the possessions, titles, and relationships you have accumulated — these are gifts of the Lord's energy, due to be returned. Begin handing them over now, in daana and in succession planning, rather than letting māyā collect them at the end.
    • When mentoring younger family members or students, do not preach against the goddesses or other paths — Prabhupāda did not. Simply keep pointing, again and again, to the difference between asking the energy for facility and asking the Energetic for service. Let your final years be that one clear signal.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the long list of names (Durgā, Kālī, Caṇḍikā, Ambikā, etc.) as proof that 'all paths are one' and that worship of the material energy is equivalent to worship of Kṛṣṇa — the verse distinguishes śāktas from Vaiṣṇavas, it does not collapse them.
    • Disrespecting Māyādevī or her worshipers as a way of feeling like a 'real' Vaiṣṇava — Kṛṣṇa Himself blesses her and assigns her these names; the Vaiṣṇava becomes a śuddha-śākta by serving the Lord with His energy, not by despising the energy.
    • Reducing 'I want spiritual life' to a slightly more refined shopping list addressed to Māyādevī — praying for a peaceful home, a good marriage, health, and success and labeling that as bhakti, when in substance it is still durgā-śākta worship dressed in Vaiṣṇava clothes.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda calls Vaiṣṇavas 'śuddha-śāktas' because the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra addresses Harā, Kṛṣṇa's energy. Where in your own sādhana have you been approaching Māyādevī (asking the energy for facility) when you thought you were approaching Kṛṣṇa? Be specific — what did you actually pray for last week?
    • The verse lists fourteen names for the same Māyādevī across fourteen regions. Modern interfaith voices use this kind of list to argue 'all paths lead to the same goal.' Prabhupāda explicitly distinguishes śāktas from Vaiṣṇavas and says they sometimes have rivalry. Where do you draw the line between honoring difference and falling into a flat 'all the same' that this verse refuses?
    • Prabhupāda says people are 'generally interested in material enjoyment' and therefore worship Māyādevī under her many names. Look at your own circle — family, coworkers, the people you spiritually admire. Who is actually a Vaiṣṇava in the technical sense Prabhupāda gives, and who is, gently, a śākta? Does naming this honestly feel like discrimination or like discriminative wisdom?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a sincere relative who has just returned from a trip to Vārāṇasī, full of devotion to Durgā, and says, 'Durgā, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa — it is all one śakti, all one energy, the names don't matter. Even your Bhāgavatam lists fourteen names for the same goddess.' Student B plays the Vaiṣṇava family member who has to respond in the next two minutes — without insulting the relative's faith, without flattening the distinction Prabhupāda draws, and without retreating into 'well, you do you.' Switch roles. Then debrief: where did each of you slip into either rudeness or false agreement?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole verse and purport sound sectarian. Prabhupāda is essentially saying 'our worship is pure, theirs is material.' Isn't that exactly the kind of religious one-upmanship the modern world is trying to leave behind?
      The distinction is not sectarian, it is diagnostic. Prabhupāda is not ranking communities by birth or label — he is naming what each worshiper is actually asking for. If I approach the Lord's energy for a job, a spouse, a healthy child, a long life, I am, by definition, a śākta in that moment, regardless of which Deity I stand in front of. If I approach the same energy asking only for the chance to serve Kṛṣṇa, I am a śuddha-śākta. The line runs through each of our hearts before it runs between traditions. Far from being arrogant, this verse forces a Vaiṣṇava to constantly check whether his own prayer is actually devotional or just dressed-up viṣaya. Real respect for other paths begins with the honesty to see what is being asked for, in them and in us.
    • Why would Kṛṣṇa Himself bless His own māyā with all these glorious names and worldwide worship if māyā is the very thing keeping souls bound? It seems contradictory — the Lord is sponsoring the illusion.
      Māyā is not Kṛṣṇa's enemy; she is His faithful servant, doing exactly the work He assigns. Souls who insist on enjoying separately from Kṛṣṇa need a manager, and she is that manager — strict, generous, and impartial. By blessing her with these names, Kṛṣṇa is arranging that those who are not yet ready for direct surrender still have a structured way to grow, receive their karma, and slowly become exhausted with material enjoyment. The Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra calls out to Harā precisely because she is the one who can release the conditioned soul back to her Lord. The 'contradiction' dissolves once you see māyā as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement of tough love, not as a rival kingdom.

    The son of Rohiṇī will also be celebrated as Saṅkarṣaṇa because of being sent from the womb of Devakī to the womb of Rohiṇī. He will be called Rāma because of His ability to please all the inhabitants of Gokula, and He will be known as Balabhadra because of His extensive physical strength.
    Purport

    These are some of the reasons why Balarāma is known as Saṅkarṣaṇa, Balarāma or sometimes Rāma. In the mahā-mantra — Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare/ Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare — people sometimes object when Rāma is accepted as Balarāma. But although devotees of Lord Rāma may object, they should know that there is no difference between Balarāma and Lord Rāma. Here Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam clearly states that Balarāma is also known as Rāma ( rāmeti ). Therefore, it is not artificial for us to speak of Lord Balarāma as Lord Rāma. Jayadeva Gosvāmī also speaks of three Rāmas: Paraśurāma, Raghupati Rāma and Balarāma. All of them are Rāmas.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The son of Rohiṇī will also be celebrated as Saṅkarṣaṇa because of being sent from the womb of Devakī to the womb of Rohiṇī. He will be called Rāma because of His ability to please all the inhabitants of Gokula, and He will be known as Balabhadra because of His extensive physical strength.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He glories māyā by her relation to Gokula filled with the highest prema by speaking of another goal of Saṅkarṣaṇa’s appearance. Because of being pulled from the womb (vai is used for emphasis), and not because of withdrawing the universe during destruction in the form of Śeṣa, he will be known as Saṅkarṣaṇa. Being taken from the womb he will then give pleasure to all the people when he comes to Gokula. Thus he will be called Rāma. Because of his state of intense prema, because of his great strength of prema, he will be called Balabhadra. Instead of balabhadraṁ balocchrayāt sometimes balaṁ balavad uccrayāt is seen. This means “because he is stronger than the strong is called Bala. Rāmeti is a compound explained in the following sūtra: saha supā (Pāṇini 1.1.4)

    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Balarāma is Saṅkarṣaṇa, Rāma, and Balabhadra — the original shelter whose strength and sweetness draw every devotee toward Kṛṣṇa.
    Practical Applications
    • Chant the mahā-mantra today and consciously include Balarāma when you say 'Hare Rāma,' refusing the mistake of separating Him from Lord Rāma.
    • Before any difficult task, take shelter of Balabhadra's bala — pray for the strength to serve Kṛṣṇa rather than for strength to push your own agenda.
    • Notice one person in your day you have failed to please through pettiness or neglect, and act as Rāma — the one who delights all — by giving them sincere attention.
    Reflection Questions
    • Balarāma is called Rāma because He pleases all the inhabitants of Gokula (loka-ramaṇāt) — whose joy am I actually organizing my day around, and whose joy do I quietly resent having to consider?
    • Balarāma's transfer from Devakī's womb to Rohiṇī's is the original saṅkarṣaṇa — where in my own life has Kṛṣṇa already 'transferred' me from one situation to another for protection I did not see at the time, and am I willing to read my present circumstance the same way?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Take the 'Rāma — loka-ramaṇāt' test on your group chat for one week: are you the friend whose presence pleases people, or the one who drains the room with sarcasm, complaints, and one-upmanship? Pick one chat and watch your own messages with this question in mind.
    • Online, devotees of one form of the Lord (Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Śiva, Devī) often pile onto each other in comment sections. Decide today that you will not participate in that — and if you see a Vaiṣṇava friend doing it, send them this verse privately. Defending Kṛṣṇa by attacking Rāma-bhaktas is not bhakti; it is ahaṅkāra wearing a tilaka.
    • Balabhadra means strength used auspiciously. In the gym, in exams, in competitions — where are you cultivating bala (strength, capability) without the bhadra (the auspiciousness, the orientation toward serving others)? Name one skill you are sharpening purely to outrank a peer, and reframe how you will use it this semester.
    householder
    • Saṅkarṣaṇa was 'drawn across' from Devakī's womb to Rohiṇī's — the Lord Himself accepted being moved between mothers for a higher purpose. When your career, your spouse's needs, or your children's schooling demand that you be 'drawn across' to a city, role, or sacrifice you did not choose, remember: even the Lord submits to such transitions. Stop framing relocation, demotion, or caregiving duty as personal loss.
    • Loka-ramaṇāt at home: this week, audit whether your family experiences your arrival home as a source of ramaṇa or as the moment tension enters the house. Ask your spouse directly — and accept the answer without defending. Then, for one evening, walk in with no complaint and no agenda; just be the Rāma of that household.
    • Teach your children that the same Person bears many names. When they meet a friend whose family worships a different deity or who chants a different mantra, do not let them inherit your sectarian preferences as exclusions. Show them Jayadeva's verse: there are three Rāmas, and the Lord is not threatened by His own multiplicity.
    senior
    • Balabhadra — bala that is bhadra, strength that is auspicious. In this season, your physical bala is receding; your auspicious bala (your example, your blessings, your steadiness in chanting) is what remains and what matters. Stop mourning the first; start consciously deploying the second on the people around you.
    • You have spent decades worshipping in a particular line, with particular names. The verse asks: when you meet a devotee of another form of the Lord at this stage of life, can you greet them as a brother without the old reflex of correction? Mortality narrows the time available for sectarian distance. Drop one such grudge this month.
    • Saṅkarṣaṇa is the one who is drawn from one womb into another — a direct image of the soul's passage. As you sit with elders, with the dying, or with your own anticipation of leaving this body, meditate on this name. The Lord Himself has accepted such passages; you are not abandoned in yours. Mentor a younger devotee through their own first encounter with grief using this name as a touchstone.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the Hare Rāma portion of the mahā-mantra as referring only to Lord Rāmacandra and silently excluding Balarāma — Prabhupāda's purport directly corrects this; the verse itself (rāmeti) establishes Balarāma as Rāma.
    • Reducing Balarāma to a 'lesser' or merely supporting figure beside Kṛṣṇa, slipping into demigod-confusion — He is the original Saṅkarṣaṇa, the source of strength (balocchrayāt), not a secondary deity.
    • Romanticizing 'pleasing everyone' (loka-ramaṇa) as a license for people-pleasing or sentimental niceness, when the verse points to a Personality whose very presence delights devotees — not to our managing of others' moods.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Balarāma is celebrated under three names — Saṅkarṣaṇa (the one drawn across), Rāma (the one who pleases all of Gokula), and Balabhadra (the auspicious strength). Which of these three qualities is most missing in the way you currently serve your community, and which comes most naturally? Be honest with your partner about the gap.
    • Prabhupāda insists that 'devotees of Lord Rāma may object, but there is no difference between Balarāma and Lord Rāma.' Where in your own bhakti life do you cling to a preferred form, name, or lineage in a way that quietly excludes other Vaiṣṇavas? What would it cost your ego to drop the objection?
    • Loka-ramaṇāt — He is called Rāma because He pleases all the inhabitants. In your household, workplace, or saṅga, are you a source of ramaṇa (genuine pleasure) or of friction? Disagree with your partner if their self-assessment sounds too generous — push them to name one person they consistently fail to please and why.
    Role Play

    Two students are paired. Student A is a long-time worshipper of Lord Rāmacandra who has just walked into a kīrtana hall and heard the mahā-mantra being sung with 'Hare Rāma' interpreted as Balarāma. They are visibly upset and say, 'You are diluting my Lord — Rāma means Raghupati, not the cowherd's brother.' Student B is a Gauḍīya devotee who must respond — not to win the argument, but to honor the other's bhāva while gently pointing to SB 10.2.13 (rāmeti) and Jayadeva Gosvāmī's recognition of three Rāmas. After five minutes, swap roles. Debrief: where did defensiveness creep in? Where did you confuse loyalty to a name with loyalty to the Person?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole verse is just etymological trivia — explaining nicknames of a mythological character. Why should a serious modern reader care that 'Saṅkarṣaṇa' means 'drawn across'?
      The names of the Lord are not labels we attach from outside; they are revelations of activity. Saṅkarṣaṇa names the act of being drawn from one womb to another — meaning the Lord submits Himself to the same passage we fear most, the transition between bodies and wombs, and does so willingly to protect His devotees. Rāma names the fact that His presence produces ramaṇa, real pleasure, in everyone around Him — not the manufactured pleasure of viṣaya. Balabhadra names auspicious strength, not raw power. Each name is a meditation. To dismiss this as trivia is to assume names are arbitrary; in the Vaiṣṇava view, the name is non-different from the named, and studying why He bears each name is itself sādhana.
    • Prabhupāda is just defending the ISKCON chant against Rāma-bhaktas who disagree with him. This is sectarian apologetics, not scripture.
      Notice that Prabhupāda does not appeal to his own authority — he appeals to Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam itself (rāmeti) and to Jayadeva Gosvāmī, a pre-Caitanya ācārya revered across Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas, who openly speaks of three Rāmas: Paraśurāma, Raghupati, and Balarāma. The point is not to win a turf war but to dissolve a false objection that would set one form of the Lord against another. A genuine Rāma-bhakta, on hearing Jayadeva, has no ground left to stand on. What looks like sectarian defense is actually the opposite — an insistence that the Personality of Godhead is one, even when His names and forms are many. Demigod-confusion runs in the other direction; here, the verse protects us from the equally serious error of fragmenting the one Lord into rival deities.

    Thus instructed by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Yoga-māyā immediately agreed. With the Vedic mantra om, she confirmed that she would do what He asked. Thus having accepted the order of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, she circumambulated Him and started for the place on earth known as Nanda-gokula. There she did everything just as she had been told.
    Purport

    After receiving the orders of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Yoga-māyā twice confirmed her acceptance by saying, “Yes, sir, I shall do as You order,” and then saying om. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura comments that om signifies Vedic confirmation. Thus Yoga-māyā very faithfully received the Lord’s order as a Vedic injunction. It is a fact that whatever is spoken by the Supreme Personality of Godhead is a Vedic injunction that no one should neglect. In Vedic injunctions there are no mistakes, illusions, cheating or imperfection. Unless one understands the authority of the Vedic version, there is no purpose in quoting śāstra. No one should violate the Vedic injunctions. Rather, one should strictly execute the orders given in the Vedas. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (16.24) : tasmāc chāstraṁ pramāṇaṁ te kāryākārya-vyavasthitau jñātvā śāstra-vidhānoktaṁ karma kartum ihārhasi “One should understand what is duty and what is not duty by the regulations of the scriptures. Knowing such rules and regulations, one should act so that one may gradually be elevated.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Thus instructed by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Yogamāyā immediately agreed. With the Vedic mantra oṁ, she confirmed that she would do what He asked. Thus having accepted the order of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, she circumambulated Him and started for the place on earth known as Nanda-gokula. There she did everything just as she had been told.
    Commentary

    Saying "tatha iti" and then "om iti" is a sign of respect for the Lord. First she accepted the words, then she did parikrama , and then went to the earth (gam), one act following the other.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She acted according to what the Lord said (tathā), not deviating at all.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She obeyed because he was the supreme Lord (bhagavatā). She circumambulated him to fulfill his order. She acted according to what the Lord said (tathā), not deviating at all.

    Receive Kṛṣṇa's word as Yoga-māyā did — with om and immediate execution; His instruction is itself the Vedic injunction, free of flaw.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one direct instruction from śāstra or guru you have been softening, and execute it today exactly as given — no edits, no delay.
    • Before acting on any opinion or trend, test it against śāstra-pramāṇa; refuse to treat your preference as equal in authority to Kṛṣṇa's word.
    • When you receive an order in your sva-dharma today (from guru, scripture, or duty), answer inwardly with 'tathā' and then circumambulate it with full attention before beginning.
    Reflection Questions
    • When the Lord — through guru, śāstra, or sādhu — gives me a clear instruction, where do I delay, negotiate, or 'think it over' instead of responding with Yoga-māyā's immediate 'tathā' and 'om'?
    • What scriptural injunction do I currently treat as optional or open to interpretation, and what would change today if I received it as a Vedic order containing no mistake, illusion, or imperfection?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a teacher, parent, or senior devotee gives you a clear instruction this week — about study, screen time, or company — practice Yoga-māyā's two-stage acceptance: first say it back ('yes, I will do X by Y'), then actually start within the hour. Notice how often you skip stage two.
    • Pick one śāstric instruction you've been quietly editing to fit your social life — maybe avoiding intoxication at a party, not gossiping about a classmate, or finishing your japa before opening Instagram. For seven days, treat it as a non-negotiable Vedic injunction, not a suggestion. Journal the resistance.
    • Yoga-māyā circumambulated Kṛṣṇa before acting. Before your next exam or important task, take 60 seconds to formally offer it — not as a vague 'good vibes' gesture, but as a deliberate act of placing the work under His order. See if the quality of your effort changes.
    householder
    • Identify one family decision currently in limbo — a move, a school choice, a financial commitment, a difficult conversation with a parent. Bring it to śāstra and to a senior devotee, get a clear direction, and then execute it with Yoga-māyā's tathā-oṁ within a defined timeframe. Stop polling for a fifth opinion.
    • Audit your weekly schedule against the orders you've actually received — from guru, from scripture, from the duties of gṛhastha-āśrama. Where are you treating Kṛṣṇa's instructions as flexible while treating your work calendar as fixed? Reverse one such inversion this month.
    • When you give an instruction to your child or a junior at work, model the acceptance you want from them: visibly accept a small instruction from your own spouse or senior with the same fullness you expect. Children learn the verse by watching you live it, not by hearing you quote it.
    senior
    • At this stage the orders coming to you are increasingly subtle — a doctor's restriction, a body's limitation, a scripture's call to vairāgya and Kṛṣṇa-smaraṇa. Pick the one you have been most resisting and accept it this week with the formality of Yoga-māyā: spoken acceptance, then immediate action.
    • Mentor one younger devotee specifically on the discipline of receiving instruction. Share a story (truthfully) of an order from your guru or śāstra that you initially negotiated with, and what the cost of the delay was. Your honest history is more useful to them than your polished advice.
    • Use the loosening of worldly responsibility to deepen Vedic obedience, not to relax it. Set a daily sādhana — japa rounds, Bhāgavatam reading, a fixed hour of seva — and treat it as a non-negotiable injunction from Kṛṣṇa Himself. The body's decline is the Lord's instruction to redirect; receive it with oṁ, not with grief.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Yoga-māyā's instant acceptance as blind obedience and using that as an excuse to suspend discrimination toward unauthorized 'orders' — forgetting that her surrender was specifically to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, not to any voice claiming authority.
    • Quoting śāstra selectively to win arguments while privately ignoring the injunctions that inconvenience us — the very 'no purpose in quoting śāstra' Prabhupāda warns against.
    • Mistaking circumambulation, chanting om, and ritual confirmation for actual execution — Yoga-māyā went to Gokula and 'did everything just as she had been told,' but we often stop at the 'yes, sir' and never reach the doing.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Yoga-māyā says 'tathā' and then 'oṁ' — a double confirmation before she even moves. Share with your partner one instruction from your guru, parent, or scripture that you 'agreed' to but never actually executed. What was the gap between your tathā and your oṁ?
    • Prabhupāda says 'whatever is spoken by the Supreme Personality of Godhead is a Vedic injunction that no one should neglect.' Where in your life do you quietly negotiate with śāstra — keeping the parts that fit your lifestyle and softening the parts that don't? Be specific; don't let your group settle for a generic answer.
    • Yoga-māyā circumambulates Kṛṣṇa before leaving — she does not just nod and walk off. Discuss: what would it look like to add a parikramā-like ritual of acceptance to the orders you receive (from guru, śāstra, even your boss)? Does anyone in the group think this is performative rather than substantive — and why?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a senior devotee who has just been asked by their temple president to relocate to another city to help open a new preaching center — a clear, direct instruction with scriptural and guru sanction. Student A has career plans, a comfortable apartment, and a circle of friends here. Student B is Student A's close godbrother/godsister, sitting with them the evening after the request was made. Student B's job is NOT to convince or comfort, but to surface — using this verse — the difference between Yoga-māyā's tathā-oṁ acceptance and Student A's actual internal response. Run for 7 minutes, then switch. Debrief: where did the conversation drift toward 'finding a compromise' and away from the verse's standard?

    Objections & Responses
    • Yoga-māyā is a divine personality with no material conditioning. It's unrealistic — even unfair — to hold ordinary conditioned souls to her standard of instant, unquestioning acceptance. Doesn't this verse just describe a transcendental transaction that has nothing to do with us?
      It is precisely because she is liberated that she is shown to us — she is the model, not the exception. The Bhāgavatam does not record her acceptance to entertain us; it records it so that we may calibrate our own response. Yes, our acceptance will be halting, partial, mixed with doubt — but the *direction* must be hers. The Gauḍīya path does not ask us to already be Yoga-māyā; it asks us to stop pretending that our negotiation with the Lord's order is somehow more sophisticated than her simple oṁ. Begin by noticing the gap, not by excusing it.
    • 'No one should violate the Vedic injunctions' sounds like religious authoritarianism. In a world where scriptures have been used to justify caste oppression, gender hierarchy, and worse, isn't blind acceptance of śāstra dangerous? Shouldn't we test every injunction against reason and conscience?
      The verse Prabhupāda quotes — tasmāc chāstraṁ pramāṇaṁ te — does not abolish discrimination; it locates it. Reason is the instrument by which we understand śāstra, not the tribunal that overrules it. The Gauḍīya teacher would point out two things. First, what gets called 'śāstra' in the abuses you mention is usually smṛti misapplied, cultural accretion, or self-interest dressed in Sanskrit — not the direct words of Kṛṣṇa, which are what this purport is about. Second, the modern alternative — every individual conscience as final authority — has produced its own catastrophes. The question is not whether to accept an authority above your own preference, but which one. Yoga-māyā chose Kṛṣṇa. The verse invites you to examine what you have chosen.

    When the child of Devakī was attracted and transferred into the womb of Rohiṇī by Yoga-māyā, Devakī seemed to have a miscarriage. Thus all the inhabitants of the palace loudly lamented, “Alas, Devakī has lost her child!”
    Purport

    “All the inhabitants of the palace” includes Kaṁsa. When everyone lamented, Kaṁsa joined in compassion, thinking that perhaps because of drugs or some other external means, Devakī had undergone this abortion. The real story of what happened after Yoga-māyā attracted the child of Devakī into the womb of Rohiṇī in the seventh month of Rohiṇī’s pregnancy is described as follows in the Hari-vaṁśa. At midnight, while Rohiṇī was deeply sleeping, she experienced, as if in a dream, that she had undergone a miscarriage. After some time, when she awoke, she saw that this had indeed happened, and she was in great anxiety. But Yoga-māyā then informed her, “O auspicious lady, your child is now being replaced. I am attracting a child from the womb of Devakī, and therefore your child will be known as Saṅkarṣaṇa.” The word yoga-nidrā is significant. When one is spiritually reconnected through self-realization, one regards his material life as having been like a dream. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (2.69) : yā niśā sarva-bhūtānāṁ tasyāṁ jāgarti saṁyamī yasyāṁ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ “What is night for all beings is the time of awakening for the self-controlled; and the time of awakening for all beings is night for the introspective sage.” The stage of self-realization is called yoga-nidrā. All material activities appear to be a dream when one is spiritually awakened. Thus yoga-nidrā may be explained to be Yoga-māyā.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the child of Devakī was attracted and transferred into the womb of Rohiṇī by Yogamāyā, Devakī seemed to have a miscarriage. Thus all the inhabitants of the palace loudly lamented, "Alas, Devakī has lost her child!"
    Commentary

    Concerning the apparent miscarriage, the citizens suspected that Kamsa must have done so black magic to cause the miscarriage. The citizens of Mathura began to lament out of affection for Devaki.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Yoganidrā means Yogamāyā since sleep takes away the intelligence of all people. Yogamāyā did this with great skill (praṇīte) so that Devakī would not suffer, Rohiṇī would not be astonished, and the people could not see it happen. One should understand the sequence of events according to Hari-vaṁśa. Vasudeva first placed the child in Devakī’s womb and Rohiṇī then went Gokula. In the seventh month of pregnancy the embryo was transferred from Devakī to Rohiṇī. The Lord speaks to Yogamāyā in Hari-vaṁśa: saptamo devakī-garho yo ‘ṁśaḥ saumyo mamāgrajaḥ sa saṁktrāmiyitavyas te saptame māsi rohinīm The seventh child of Devakī who is expansion and my elder brother was transferred to the womb of Rohiṇī in the seventh month of pregnancy. Then method of transfer is described in detail: sārdharātre sthitaṁ garbham pātayantī rajasvalā nidrayā sahasāvisṭā papāta dharaṇī-tale sā svapnam iva taṁ dṛsṭvā svagarbhe garbham āhitaṁ apaśyantī ca taṁ garbhaṁ muhūrtam vyatitā ‘bhavat tām āha nidrā-saṁvignāṁ naiśe tamasi rohiṇīm kaṛṣaṇenāsya garbhasya svagarbhe cāhitasya vai saṇkarṣaṇo nāma śubhe tave putro bhaviṣyati In the middle of the night Devakī aborted her child and fell on the ground unconscious. As if in a dream she saw the child come out of her womb and felt pain for some moments on seeing her child. Yogamāyā spoke to Rohiṇī in the darkness of night, as she slept. “The child taken from another womb and placed in your womb will be your son named Saṅkarṣaṇa.” Aho indicates amazement or lamentation. They understood that the child had been aborted out of fear of Kaṁsa. Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: saptamo bhoja-rājasya bhayād rodhoparodhataḥ devakhyāḥ patito garbh iti loko vadisyati The people said that the seventh child of Devakī had been aborted out of fear of Kaṁsa, which had caused great damage. Or, Kaṁsa somehow caused the child to be aborted. They did not speak this directly, out of fear of Kaṁsa, but gossiped among themselves in loud voices.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Shraddha (Faith / Reverence)Daksya (Resourcefulness / Skill)Nyaya (Justice / Righteous Judgment)Arjava (Simplicity / Straightforwardness)Brahmacharya (Self-discipline / Restraint)Adambhitva (Non-hypocrisy / Authenticity)Shaucha (Cleanliness / Purity)Dhairya (Composure / Courage)
    Related verses
    SB 10.2.13 SB 10.2.14 SB 10.2.16 SB 10.2.17 SB 10.2.18 BG 9.11 BG 15.2 BG 6.47 BG 5.4 BG 9.1 BG 4.24
    Concepts
    JivaYoga
    Personal Guidance
    Yoga-māyā shifts the child unseen — what looks like loss to worldly eyes is Kṛṣṇa's arrangement; the awakened soul sees through the dream.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one event today you've been mourning as 'loss' and ask honestly where Kṛṣṇa's hand may be arranging something unseen.
    • Refuse to join the crowd's lamentation reflex — pause before reacting to bad news and remember yoga-nidrā: material life is dream-like to the awakened.
    • Spend ten minutes in japa or scriptural reading tonight to practice the muni's reversal — waking to Kṛṣṇa while the world sleeps in viṣaya.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my own life have I mistaken Yoga-māyā's protective rearrangement for loss — what 'miscarriage' did I once mourn that was actually Kṛṣṇa's hand quietly relocating something for safekeeping?
    • Like Kaṁsa joining the lament out of material compassion while missing the real spiritual reality, where am I outwardly sympathizing with surface events while remaining blind to the deeper movement of Kṛṣṇa's plan?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time your friend group collectively 'laments' over something — a breakup, a bad grade, someone not getting into the college they wanted. Join the comfort, but privately ask: am I grieving for their soul's situation or just for the social-media-shaped version of their disappointment? Offer one sentence that points beyond the surface, even if it costs you a little coolness.
    • Yoga-nidrā means being awake while others sleep. Pick one thing your peers are obsessively awake to right now (a streaming series everyone is bingeing, a discourse cycle, a comparison spiral on Instagram) and consciously 'sleep' through it for one week — no consumption, no commentary. Use the reclaimed attention for japa, reading, or a real conversation with a parent.
    • Before your next exam or interview, do the work fully — but the night before, formally hand the result over to Kṛṣṇa the way Yoga-māyā handled the transfer: not your project to micromanage. If you fail, you are still being moved by His arrangement; if you succeed, the credit was never yours to claim.
    householder
    • When a family member is suffering — a child failing at school, a spouse stressed at work, an aging parent declining — pause before reacting like 'all the inhabitants of the palace.' Ask: is my distress karuṇā for their soul, or panic about my own identity as good-parent, good-spouse, good-child? Then act from the first, not the second.
    • Money, promotions, and home decisions often feel like they require frantic management. Practice one major family decision this month where you do your sva-dharma fully — research, discuss, decide — and then explicitly entrust the outcome to Kṛṣṇa, the way Vasudeva and Devakī had to trust Yoga-māyā's arrangement when the child seemed lost. Watch how this changes the temperature of the household.
    • Your children are watching which 'losses' devastate you. If you collapse over a missed bonus or a dented car, you are teaching them that the body and its extensions are the self. Choose one such 'loss' this quarter and respond visibly as a dhīra — name it as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement at the dinner table, without preaching.
    senior
    • The body's 'transfer' is no longer abstract for you. Each morning, sit for five minutes and rehearse the truth that Yoga-māyā is already arranging your next ashram — your job is to remain a willing instrument, not a frightened palace-dweller. Let this steady the day's smaller fears.
    • Loosen one attachment publicly this season — give away a possession, hand a responsibility to a younger person, release a grudge by name. Do not narrate it as renunciation; simply let it go, the way the womb released the child. Mentor someone by showing them what unclenched hands look like.
    • When juniors lament around you — over careers, marriages, illnesses — resist the pull to join the chorus. Offer the dhīra-bhāva: a calm word that points to Kṛṣṇa's arrangement, a verse you have lived with, a story from your own life where what looked like loss was Yoga-māyā's transfer. Your composure at this stage is itself the teaching.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading yoga-nidrā as a poetic metaphor for mindfulness or 'being present,' rather than as the awakened state in which all material life is recognized as a dream and Kṛṣṇa as the only reality.
    • Sentimentalizing Devakī's apparent loss into a generic lesson about grief, while ignoring the verse's actual point that Yoga-māyā was actively protecting Kṛṣṇa — and missing that what looks like calamity is often the Lord's arrangement.
    • Imitating Kaṁsa's external compassion — performing concern for others' bodily setbacks while inwardly indifferent to their spiritual welfare — and calling it karuṇā.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa wept along with the palace when he heard of the 'miscarriage' — his compassion was real in the moment, yet rooted in misunderstanding. Share a time you offered sincere sympathy that, in hindsight, was actually karuṇā for the body rather than for the soul. What would real compassion have looked like instead, and where do you disagree with each other about that line?
    • The verse turns on yoga-nidrā — the seer is awake to what others sleep through, and asleep to what they chase. Name one area of your life where the people around you are 'awake' (career anxiety, relationship drama, political news) and you sense Kṛṣṇa is asking you to 'sleep.' Push back on each other: is this genuine vairāgya, or is it spiritual bypassing of a duty you owe?
    • Yoga-māyā moved the child without anyone's consent — Devakī, Rohiṇī, and the palace were all 'deceived' for a higher purpose. Discuss: when, if ever, is it acceptable for a devotee to allow others to misperceive a situation for the sake of a deeper good? Where does each of you draw the line between Yoga-māyā's protective concealment and ordinary dishonesty (violating satya)?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a devotee whose elderly father has just been diagnosed with a terminal illness. The doctors recommend an aggressive, painful treatment that will extend bodily life by perhaps six months. Student A senses the father is ready to turn inward toward Kṛṣṇa and would prefer to use that time in remembrance, kīrtana, and family. Student B is Student A's sibling — not a devotee — who is openly weeping like 'all the inhabitants of the palace,' insisting that anything less than the full treatment is abandonment and cruelty. Role-play the conversation. Student A must articulate the difference between karuṇā for the body and karuṇā for the soul without being cold, condescending, or hiding behind Sanskrit. Student B must press hard on what looks, from outside, like a failure of duty (kartavya) and even of love. The teacher pauses the scene at the moment of greatest tension and asks the class: where is each person right? Where is each person being moved by Yoga-māyā's covering, and where by her revealing?

    Objections & Responses
    • This story is mythological window-dressing for what was simply a miscarriage. Reading divine fetal-transfer into it is exactly the kind of magical thinking that keeps religion from being taken seriously by intelligent modern people.
      We are not asked to swap one ideology for another; we are asked to look at what the text actually claims and what it predicts. The Bhāgavata is consistent: Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Personality of Godhead, and His potencies — Yoga-māyā among them — act in history when His descent requires it. If you grant the premise that Kṛṣṇa is who the text says He is, the protective concealment of Balarāma's transfer is no more 'magical' than a parent moving a sleeping child to a safer room. The deeper question for you is not whether the event is plausible to a materialist, but whether the materialist frame itself accounts for the lived experience of devotees across centuries who have found this Kṛṣṇa to be personally responsive. Test the personalist hypothesis on its own terms — chant, hear, serve — before ruling it out by a frame imported from elsewhere.
    • Yoga-māyā deceives Kaṁsa, deceives the palace, even leaves Rohiṇī to wake up confused. Isn't this divinely sanctioned dishonesty? How can a tradition that prizes satya celebrate a cover-up?
      Satya in our line is not the flat reporting of sense-data; it is speaking and acting in accordance with the highest reality, which is Kṛṣṇa and His pleasure. Yoga-māyā's concealment of Balarāma is not a lie told to harm — it is a mother's hand placed over a child's mouth so that the assassin in the next room does not hear him cry. Kaṁsa's 'compassion' was already operating inside a deeper deception: the illusion that he was the controller, that he could kill the unkillable. Yoga-māyā did not introduce falsehood into a true situation; she protected truth (the descent of Saṅkarṣaṇa) from being destroyed by a man committed to a much larger lie. For us as practitioners, the takeaway is not 'deceive when convenient' but 'arrange your speech and silence in service of Kṛṣṇa, not in service of appearances.' That is the demanding form of satya the verse teaches.
